kdotpy: 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory on a lattice for simulating semiconductor band structures

Wouter Beugeling1,2⋆⁣†\star\dagger, Florian Bayer1,2, Christian Berger1,2, Jan Böttcher3, Leonid Bovkun1,2, Christopher Fuchs1,2, Maximilian Hofer1,2, Saquib Shamim1,2, Moritz Siebert1,2, Li-Xian Wang1,2, Ewelina M. Hankiewicz3, Tobias Kießling1,2, Hartmut Buhmann1,2 and Laurens W. Molenkamp1,2

1 Physikalisches Institut (EP3), Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland, 97074 Würzburg, Germany

2 Institute for Topological Insulators, Am Hubland, 97074 Würzburg, Germany

3 Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik (TP4), Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland, 97074 Würzburg, Germany

⋆\star kdotpy@uni-wuerzburg.de , †\dagger wouter.beugeling@physik.uni-wuerzburg.de

Abstract

The software project kdotpy provides a Python application for simulating electronic band structures of semiconductor devices with 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory on a lattice. The application implements the widely used Kane model, capable of reliable predictions of transport and optical properties for a large variety of topological and non-topological materials with a zincblende crystal structure. The application automates the tedious steps of simulating band structures. The user inputs the relevant physical parameters on the command line, for example materials and dimensions of the device, magnetic field, and temperature. The program constructs the appropriate matrix Hamiltonian on a discretized lattice of spatial coordinates and diagonalizes it. The physical observables are extracted from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors and saved as output. The program is highly customizable with a large set of configuration options and material parameters.

The project is released as free open source software under the GNU General Public License, version 3. The code that accompanies this article is available from our Gitlab repository at https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/kdotpy/kdotpy/-/tags/v1.0.0.

1 Introduction

In the field of solid-state physics, particularly in the branch of semiconductor physics, the theory of electronic band structures plays a central role. Semiconductor materials are inherently very complex systems due to the typically large number of atomic orbitals of their constituent atoms. A reduction to the essential degrees of freedom (namely, the electronic bands close to the Fermi level at charge neutrality) can be achieved by effective models, such as the perturbative method known as 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory. The Kane model [1], a 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory that was originally proposed for describing the electronic band structure of indium antimonide (InSb), has since become an established model for the large category of binary semiconductor compounds with zincblende crystal structure, and in particular for narrow gap semiconductor compounds. The Kane model has been widely used in the semiconductor community, because the resulting band structures are well suited for predicting transport phenomena as well as optical (spectroscopic) properties. It is therefore not only a valuable asset upon analyzing data, but also a very powerful tool for designing device functionality.

The minimal number of the degrees of freedom in the Kane model is still too large to permit exact analytic solutions of the Schrödinger equation, that defines the band structure. The problem can be approached numerically, but setting up numerical simulations and extracting physical observables can be a tedious task, for example due to the quantity and complexity of the matrix elements in the Hamiltonian. These issues mandate a software solution where the tedious tasks are automated, i.e., an application which takes physical parameters like geometry and materials of a device as input, and which produces physical observables as its output.

Here, we present the Python application kdotpy as a means to deal with these challenges. The motivation for developing kdotpy has been the need to analyze the experimental results of the research group of L. W. Molenkamp in Würzburg. In many regards the situation that triggered the development of kdotpy was archetypical for an experimental group engaged in the study of sophisticated semiconductor heterostructures. The complexity of the collected data called for a description beyond simplified effective models. It was well understood that 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory provided a suitable framework for a realistic description of the experimental findings and a Fortran program set up by Pfeuffer-Jeschke and Novik [2, 3] was already used for band structure simulations for many years. However, the modelling used in this program proved to be inadequate for simulating edge channels and surface states. Moreover, it lacks an intuitive user interface, and the program structure and the programming style have proven to be major obstacles towards maintainability and towards future extension. In particular, the fact that the initial developers had moved on to other positions and a general lack of detail in the documentation of the code constitute major entrance thresholds for inclusion of novel functionalities.

In the kdotpy project, we attempt to steer clear of these problems by applying modern concepts regarding project design and development workflow. The development strategy is guided by the philosophy that kdotpy’s primary goal is to support current (experimental and theoretical) research, for which feedback from the community is an important aspect. While kdotpy has started out with the specific task of analyzing transport phenomena in Mn-doped HgTe quantum wells [4, 5, 6], it has since been extended to tackle a much broader variety of problems [7, 8, 9, 10]. As 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory is much more widely applicable than the study of topological insulators or HgTe in particular, we have equipped kdotpy with the infrastructure for simulating any material whose band structure is described by the Kane model. This includes other II-VI materials as well as III-V semiconductors like GaAs and InSb. We expect that kdotpy will thus be beneficial for a broad community spanning various disciplines in semiconductor physics. We intend to create a diverse and international user base and encourage active discussion among users and developers, in the spirit of open science and open software development. The community driven nature facilitates sustainable maintenance and future project development.

In line with modern standards in scientific research, we strive towards transparency by publishing this project as open source software. We believe that the choice of Python as a widely known programming language facilitates inspection of our code and thus fits the ideas of open science. We aim for a high level of reproducibility and for compliance with the FAIR principles for research data [11] by providing rich metadata in the output files and by avoiding the use of proprietary file formats.

The purpose of this article is to provide a comprehensive overview of all important components of kdotpy together with relevant physical background. We emphasize that reading the complete manuscript is not required for being able to use the application: We encourage the reader to focus on the parts of personal interest and/or those needed to address a specific physical problem. The article is structured as follows: In Sec. 2, we provide an in-depth review of the physical concepts and theories essential for understanding the implementation. In Sec. 3, we discuss all important components of the implementation, making the connection between the physics and the project’s source code. Installation instructions are provided in Sec. 4. We illustrate the usage of kdotpy with several detailed examples in Sec. 5. The Appendices contain technical details of the implementation as well as a comprehensive reference of configuration options, material parameters, command-line arguments, and several other aspects.

2 Physics background

The Kane model [1] implemented in kdotpy was originally proposed as a theory for the electronic band structure of InSb. It has proven to be a suitable model for a broad class of binary semiconductor compounds with a zincblende crystal structure, to which InSb also belongs. The Kane model defines an 𝟖×𝟖8\times 8 Hamiltonian depending on the momentum coordinate 𝐤\mathbf{k}. The basis of the Hilbert space is formed by two 𝒔s orbitals and six 𝒑p orbitals. These states are treated exactly at the �\Gamma point (𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=0), while couplings to other (so-called remote) bands are treated perturbatively in the framework of 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory.

Importantly, the Kane model takes into account spin-orbit interaction, which is essential for explaining the energetic positions of the electronic bands at the �\Gamma point [1]. In compounds of heavy elements, spin-orbit coupling and other relativistic effects become strong enough to result in an inversion of the band ordering. The latter is the key ingredient for the formation of topological phases, which constitute a major research branch at the Department of Physics in Würzburg since the first experimental realizations of such materials in mercury telluride (HgTe) quantum wells [12]. 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory is well suited towards accessing topological properties and accordingly this was a main focus upon setting up the kdotpy project.

The numerical approach also admits analysis of more complicated configurations than bulk materials. In particular, experiments are typically performed with devices with several layers of zincblende-type materials stacked on top of a substrate. The latter constellation is described by taking the bulk Hamiltonian and substituting the momentum coordinate 𝒌𝒛k_{z} by its spatial representation −𝐢˜​𝒉∂𝒛-\mathrm{i}\mathord{\mathchar 126h}\partial_{z}, a derivative with respect to the spatial coordinate 𝒛z. For simulating the band structure, the 𝒛z coordinate is discretized to a finite set {𝒛𝒋}\{z_{j}\}, so that the Hilbert space dimension (and the size of the Hamiltonian matrix) becomes 𝟖​𝒏𝒛8n_{z}. The different layers in the system are modelled by making the coefficients in the Kane model 𝒛z-dependent. This approach goes back to Burt [13, 14] and has since been used by many others, see, e.g., Refs. [2, 3, 15]. This discretization method distinguishes kdotpy from the aforementioned Fortran program [2, 3], which uses an expansion into Legendre polynomials in order to convert the Hamiltonian to matrix form. The present approach has the benefits that the modelling is more intuitive and that it can more reliably resolve essential features like edge channels [4] and surface states [7].

The bulk Kane model and the reduction to lower dimensional geometries are discussed Secs. 2.1 and 2.2, respectively. The remainder of Sec. 2 is dedicated to the effects of magnetic fields, bulk inversion asymmetry, and strain, as well as to topology.

2.1 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory and the Kane model in a nutshell

2.1.1 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory

The 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} method aims at finding an effective model for the band structure near a high-symmetry point. The method is based on perturbation theory on the Bloch wave functions, where eigenenergies and eigenstates at 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=0 are treated as exact and the contributions for 𝐤≠𝟎\mathbf{k}\not=0 as perturbation. The Schrödinger equation [𝐩^𝟐/𝟐𝒎+𝑽(𝐫)](𝐫)𝒏,𝐤=𝑬𝒏(𝐤)(𝐫)𝒏,𝐤[\hat{\mathbf{p}}^{2}/2m+V(\mathbf{r})]{}_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=E_{n}(\mathbf{k}){}_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) acting on the Bloch wave functions (𝐫)𝒏,𝐤=𝐞𝐢𝐤⋅𝐫𝒖𝒏,𝐤(𝐫){}_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}u_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) can be written in terms of the Bloch functions 𝒖𝒏,𝐤​(𝐫)u_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) as

[˜​𝒉𝟐​𝐤𝟐𝟐​𝒎+𝟐​˜​𝒉​𝐤⋅𝐩^𝟐​𝒎+𝐩^𝟐𝟐​𝒎+𝑽⁡(𝐫)]​𝒖𝒏,𝐤​(𝐫)=𝑬𝒏​(𝐤)​𝒖𝒏,𝐤​(𝐫),\left[\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}\mathbf{k}^{2}}{2m}+\frac{2\mathord{\mathchar 126h}\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}}{2m}+\frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}^{2}}{2m}+V(\mathbf{r})\right]u_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=E_{n}(\mathbf{k})u_{n,\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}), (1)

where 𝐩^=−𝐢˜​𝒉∇\hat{\mathbf{p}}=-\mathrm{i}\mathord{\mathchar 126h}\nabla is the momentum operator, 𝐤\mathbf{k} is a vector of real values, and the index 𝒏n labels the bands. The Hamiltonian 𝑯𝟎=𝐩^/𝟐​𝒎+𝑽⁡(𝐫)H_{0}=\hat{\mathbf{p}}/2m+V(\mathbf{r}) at 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=0 is treated as exact, whereas 𝑯𝐤′=˜​𝒉𝟐​𝐤𝟐/𝟐​𝒎+˜​𝒉​𝐤⋅𝐩^/𝒎H^{\prime}_{\mathbf{k}}=\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}\mathbf{k}^{2}/2m+\mathord{\mathchar 126h}\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}/m is treated as perturbation. The second term in 𝑯𝐤′H^{\prime}_{\mathbf{k}} gives 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory its name. The unperturbed eigenenergies 𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)E_{n}(0) and eigenfunctions |𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩\lvert u_{n,0}\rangle, that solve 𝑯𝟎|𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩=𝑬𝒏(𝟎)|𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩H_{0}\lvert u_{n,0}\rangle=E_{n}(0)\lvert u_{n,0}\rangle, are assumed to be known. The first order perturbation to the energy is

𝑬𝒏(𝟏)​(𝐤)=⟨𝒖𝒏,𝟎|𝑯𝐤′|𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩=˜​𝒉𝟐​𝐤𝟐𝟐​𝒎.E_{n}^{(1)}(\mathbf{k})=\langle u_{n,0}|H^{\prime}_{\mathbf{k}}|u_{n,0}\rangle=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}\mathbf{k}^{2}}{2m}. (2)

An additional term proportional to ⟨𝒖𝒏,𝟎|𝐤⋅𝐩^|𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩\langle u_{n,0}|\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}|u_{n,0}\rangle vanishes if we assume that the dispersions attain a maximum or minimum at 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=0. The first order perturbation to the eigenfunctions is

|𝒖𝒏,𝐤(𝟏)⟩=˜​𝒉𝒎∑𝒏′:𝑬𝒏′≠𝑬𝒏𝐤⋅𝐏𝒏′​𝒏𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)−𝑬𝒏′​(𝟎)|𝒖𝒏′,𝟎⟩,\lvert u_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{(1)}\rangle=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{m}\sum_{n^{\prime}:E_{n^{\prime}}\not=E_{n}}\frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n}}{E_{n}(0)-E_{n^{\prime}}(0)}\lvert u_{n^{\prime},0}\rangle, (3)

where 𝐏𝒏′​𝒏≡⟨𝒖𝒏′,𝟎|𝐩^|𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n}\equiv\langle u_{n^{\prime},0}|\hat{\mathbf{p}}|u_{n,0}\rangle and the sum runs over all bands 𝒏′n^{\prime} for which 𝑬𝒏′​(𝟎)≠𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)E_{n^{\prime}}(0)\not=E_{n}(0). From Eq. (3), we obtain the second order perturbation of the energy as

𝑬𝒏(𝟐)(𝐤)=⟨𝒖𝒏,𝟎|𝑯𝐤′|𝒖𝒏,𝐤(𝟏)⟩=˜​𝒉𝟐𝒎𝟐∑𝒏′:𝑬𝒏′≠𝑬𝒏|𝐤⋅𝐏𝒏′​𝒏|𝟐𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)−𝑬𝒏′​(𝟎)+𝓞(𝐤𝟑),E_{n}^{(2)}(\mathbf{k})=\langle u_{n,0}|H^{\prime}_{\mathbf{k}}|u^{(1)}_{n,\mathbf{k}}\rangle=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}}{m^{2}}\sum_{n^{\prime}:E_{n^{\prime}}\not=E_{n}}\frac{\lvert\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n}\rvert^{2}}{E_{n}(0)-E_{n^{\prime}}(0)}+\mathcal{O}(\mathbf{k}^{3}), (4)

noting that 𝐏𝒏​𝒏′=𝐏𝒏′​𝒏∗\mathbf{P}_{nn^{\prime}}=\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n}^{*} and discarding terms of cubic order in momentum. This observation completes the perturbation theory up to lowest nontrivial order in momentum, as

𝑬𝒏​(𝐤)\displaystyle E_{n}(\mathbf{k}) =𝑬𝒏(𝟎)+˜​𝒉𝟐​𝐤𝟐𝟐​𝒎+˜​𝒉𝟐𝒎𝟐∑𝒏′:𝑬𝒏′≠𝑬𝒏|𝐤⋅𝐏𝒏′​𝒏|𝟐𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)−𝑬𝒏′​(𝟎)+𝓞(𝐤𝟑),\displaystyle=E_{n}(0)+\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}\mathbf{k}^{2}}{2m}+\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}}{m^{2}}\sum_{n^{\prime}:E_{n^{\prime}}\not=E_{n}}\frac{\lvert\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n}\rvert^{2}}{E_{n}(0)-E_{n^{\prime}}(0)}+\mathcal{O}(\mathbf{k}^{3}), (5)
|𝒖𝒏,𝐤(𝟏)⟩\displaystyle\lvert u_{n,\mathbf{k}}^{(1)}\rangle =˜​𝒉𝒎∑𝒏′:𝑬𝒏′≠𝑬𝒏𝐤⋅𝐏𝒏′​𝒏𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)−𝑬𝒏′​(𝟎)|𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩+𝓞(𝐤𝟐).\displaystyle=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{m}\sum_{n^{\prime}:E_{n^{\prime}}\not=E_{n}}\frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n}}{E_{n}(0)-E_{n^{\prime}}(0)}\lvert u_{n,0}\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\mathbf{k}^{2}). (6)

Importantly, it is possible to consider only those bands 𝒏n with energies 𝑬𝒏​(𝟎)E_{n}(0) sufficiently close to the charge neutrality point, or in other words, to reduce the number of degrees of freedom by choosing a restricted selection of the |𝒖𝒏,𝟎⟩\lvert u_{n,0}\rangle as basis. However, the perturbations involve a sum over all bands 𝒏′n^{\prime}, also those outside of the basis. These bands are known as remote bands in the context of 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory.

2.1.2 The Kane model

In the seminal paper by Kane [1], 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory was used to calculate the band structure of InSb. As a matter of fact, Kane’s model applies to many more semiconductor materials with a zincblende lattice structure. The important extra ingredient in Kane’s analysis is spin-orbit coupling, one of the relativistic corrections that affect the atomic orbitals. The Hamiltonian 𝑯𝟎H_{0} (cf. Eq. (1)) is modified by adding the spin-orbit term [1]

𝑯𝐒𝐎=˜​𝒉𝟒​𝒎𝟐​𝒄𝟐(∇𝑽×𝐩^)⋅�H_{\mathrm{SO}}=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{4m^{2}c^{2}}(\nabla V\times\hat{\mathbf{p}})\cdot\bm{\sigma} (7)

where �=(�𝒙,�𝒚,�𝒛)\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z}) is the vector of Pauli matrices acting on the spin degree of freedom and 𝑽V is the potential near the atomic core.

In InSb, the relevant atomic orbitals are the 𝟓​𝒔5s orbitals of In and the 𝟓​𝒑5p orbitals of Sb. Together with the spin degree of freedom (𝑺=𝟏𝟐S=\frac{1}{2}), this yields the eight component basis,

|𝑺,↑⟩,−𝟏𝟐|𝑿+𝐢𝒀,↓⟩,|𝒁,↑⟩,𝟏𝟐|𝑿−𝐢𝒀,↓⟩,|𝑺,↓⟩,+𝟏𝟐|𝑿−𝐢𝒀,↑⟩,|𝒁,↓⟩,𝟏𝟐|𝑿+𝐢𝒀,↑⟩,\lvert S,\mathord{\uparrow}\rangle,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert X+\mathrm{i}Y,\mathord{\downarrow}\rangle,\lvert Z,\mathord{\uparrow}\rangle,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert X-\mathrm{i}Y,\mathord{\downarrow}\rangle,\lvert S,\mathord{\downarrow}\rangle,+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert X-\mathrm{i}Y,\mathord{\uparrow}\rangle,\lvert Z,\mathord{\downarrow}\rangle,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert X+\mathrm{i}Y,\mathord{\uparrow}\rangle, (8)

where |𝑺⟩\lvert S\rangle labels the 𝒔s orbital and |𝑿⟩,|𝒀⟩,|𝒁⟩\lvert X\rangle,\lvert Y\rangle,\lvert Z\rangle the 𝒑p orbitals. In this basis, the Hamiltonian at 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=0 is represented by the diagonal matrix 𝑯𝟎=diag⁡(𝑬𝒔,𝑬𝒑,𝑬𝒑,𝑬𝒑,𝑬𝒔,𝑬𝒑,𝑬𝒑,𝑬𝒑)H_{0}=\diag(E_{s},E_{p},E_{p},E_{p},E_{s},E_{p},E_{p},E_{p}), and 𝑯𝐒𝐎H_{\mathrm{SO}} can be written as

In the basis of Eq. (10), the Hamiltonian 𝑯𝟎+𝑯𝐒𝐎H_{0}+H_{\mathrm{SO}} can be diagonalized as

𝑯𝟎+𝑯𝐒𝐎=(𝑬𝐜𝟎𝟎𝑬𝐜𝑬𝐯𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑬𝐯𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑬𝐯𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑬𝐯𝑬𝐯−�𝐒𝐎𝟎𝟎𝑬𝐯−�𝐒𝐎),H_{0}+H_{\mathrm{SO}}=\begin{pmatrix}E_{\mathrm{c}}&0&\\ 0&E_{\mathrm{c}}\\ &&E_{\mathrm{v}}&0&0&0\\ &&0&E_{\mathrm{v}}&0&0\\ &&0&0&E_{\mathrm{v}}&0\\ &&0&0&0&E_{\mathrm{v}}\\ &&&&&&E_{\mathrm{v}}-\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}&0\\ &&&&&&0&E_{\mathrm{v}}-\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}\end{pmatrix}, (11)

with 𝑬𝐜≡𝑬𝒔E_{\mathrm{c}}\equiv E_{s}, 𝑬𝐯≡𝑬𝒑+𝟏𝟑​�E_{\mathrm{v}}\equiv E_{p}+\frac{1}{3}\Delta, and 𝑬𝐯−�𝐒𝐎≡𝑬𝒑−𝟐𝟑​�E_{\mathrm{v}}-\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}\equiv E_{p}-\frac{2}{3}\Delta referring to the ‘conduction band’, ‘valence band’ and split-off band energies at �\Gamma, respectively. Note that in the notation we use the labels for ‘conduction’ and ‘valence’ band for the �𝟔\Gamma_{6} and �𝟖\Gamma_{8} bands, respectively, without regard to the actual band ordering. For inverted materials, 𝑬𝐜E_{\mathrm{c}} lies in the valence band and 𝑬𝐯E_{\mathrm{v}} in the conduction band.

We note that between references (cf. Refs. [1, 16, 2, 3], for example), the basis may differ slightly by complex phases and order. Here, we group the multiplets belonging to each representation (�𝟔\Gamma_{6}, �𝟖\Gamma_{8}, �𝟕\Gamma_{7}) together. The Hamiltonian thus has the block structure

𝑯=(𝑯𝟔𝟔𝑯𝟔𝟖𝑯𝟔𝟕𝑯𝟖𝟔𝑯𝟖𝟖𝑯𝟖𝟕𝑯𝟕𝟔𝑯𝟕𝟖𝑯𝟕𝟕).H=\left(\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}H_{66}&H_{68}&H_{67}\\ \hline\cr H_{86}&H_{88}&H_{87}\\ \hline\cr H_{76}&H_{78}&H_{77}\end{array}\right). (12)

Where necessary due to space restriction, we will write terms of the full 𝟖×𝟖8\times 8 Hamiltonian in terms of these smaller blocks.

The 𝐤⋅𝐩^\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}} term in the Hamiltonian introduces matrix elements proportional to 𝒌𝒙​⟨𝑺|𝒑𝒙|𝑿⟩k_{x}\langle S|p_{x}|X\rangle, 𝒌𝒚​⟨𝑺|𝒑𝒚|𝒀⟩k_{y}\langle S|p_{y}|Y\rangle and 𝒌𝒛​⟨𝑺|𝒑𝒛|𝒁⟩k_{z}\langle S|p_{z}|Z\rangle. To write these terms, one defines the Kane parameter

𝑷=˜​𝒉𝒎​|⟨𝑺|𝒑^𝒙|𝑿⟩|=˜​𝒉𝒎​|⟨𝑺|𝒑^𝒚|𝒀⟩|=˜​𝒉𝒎​|⟨𝑺|𝒑^𝒛|𝒁⟩|.P=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{m}\lvert\langle S|\hat{p}_{x}|X\rangle\rvert=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{m}\lvert\langle S|\hat{p}_{y}|Y\rangle\rvert=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{m}\lvert\langle S|\hat{p}_{z}|Z\rangle\rvert. (13)

The ambiguity in the definitions of 𝑷P in the literature (again, cf. Refs. [1, 16, 2, 3]) is resolved by choosing a real and positive value. The value of the Kane parameter is of similar magnitude for many materials due to the similarity of the orbital wave functions.

The next step towards the formulation of the full Kane model is to identify all possible inversion symmetric terms up to quadratic order. (We will discuss inversion asymmetric terms in Sec. 2.6.) Using the conventions of Ref. [3], we write

2.1.3 Axial symmetry

Most of the matrix elements of Eq. (16) preserve axial symmetry, i.e., they are invariant under a rotation around the 𝒛z axis. The only exception is 𝑹𝐤R_{\mathbf{k}}, which can be expanded into an axial and nonaxial part, 𝑹𝐤=𝑹𝐤𝐚𝐱+𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱R_{\mathbf{k}}=R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{ax}}+R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}} with

𝑹𝐤𝐚𝐱=˜​𝒉𝟐𝟐​𝒎𝟑𝟐(+𝟐)𝟑𝒌−𝟐,𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱=˜​𝒉𝟐𝟐​𝒎𝟑𝟐(−𝟐)𝟑𝒌+𝟐.R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{ax}}=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}}{2m}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}({}_{2}+{}_{3})k_{-}^{2},\hskip 22.99988ptR_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}}=\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}^{2}}{2m}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}({}_{2}-{}_{3})k_{+}^{2}. (17)

In some calculations, we use the axial approximation, where we approximate 𝑹𝐤≈𝑹𝐤𝐚𝐱R_{\mathbf{k}}\approx R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{ax}} and neglect the non-axial part 𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}}. We note that the non-axial contributions are significant in many cases, so that the axial approximation should be used with care. This issue will be discussed in more detail in the context of Landau levels in Sec. 2.4.

2.1.4 Band structure parameters

For the simulations in kdotpy, we use the material-dependent band structure parameters established by Refs. [2, 3], summarized in Table 1. Since kdotpy has started out as a simulation program for HgTe and CdTe, we use these materials as an example here, noting that the modelling can be applied for a much wider variety of materials. We define the band energy of the �𝟖\Gamma_{8} orbitals of unstrained HgTe as the reference energy 𝑬=𝟎E=0. Thus, 𝑬𝐯=𝟎​𝐦𝐞𝐕E_{\mathrm{v}}=0\,\mathrm{meV} for HgTe by definition. The valence band energy for CdTe is determined by the valence band offset 𝑬𝐕𝐁𝐎=−𝟓𝟕𝟎​𝐦𝐞𝐕E_{\mathrm{VBO}}=-570\,\mathrm{meV} of CdTe with respect to HgTe. (All band energies, including the valence band offset, are treated as a material parameters in this model.)

All parameters come with substantial error bars. Especially for the Luttinger parameters 1,2,3 one finds substantial variations among various literature sources [16, 17]. In order to allow for adjustments of the material parameters, we have equipped kdotpy with an interface where the values can be changed in the form of a configuration file (see Sec. 3.2.4 and Appendix B.2). We have supplied the default parameters as listed in Table 1.

For ternary compounds that are formed by alloying two binary compounds for example Hg1-xCdxTe from HgTe and CdTe, we determine the parameters by suitable interpolation. These interpolations are linear to first approximation, but higher-order corrections are typically also taken into consideration. For example, the gap energy 𝑬𝐠=𝑬𝐜−𝑬𝐯E_{\mathrm{g}}=E_{\mathrm{c}}-E_{\mathrm{v}} for Hg1-xCdxTe is

𝑬𝐠​(Hg1-xCdxTe)=−𝟑𝟎𝟑​(𝟏−𝒙)+𝟏𝟔𝟎𝟔​𝒙−𝟏𝟑𝟐​𝒙​(𝟏−𝒙)E_{\mathrm{g}}(\text{Hg${}_{1-x}$Cd${}_{x}$Te})=-303(1-x)+1606x-132x(1-x) (18)

in units of meV, at zero temperature [18, 19]. This expression is a quadratic perturbation to the linear interpolation, with the coefficient of the latter term being known as the bowing parameter. The Luttinger parameters 1,2,3 and �\kappa are approximated by cubic polynomials, approximating the result of the interpolation scheme used in Ref. [2]. In general, material parameters like 𝑬𝐠E_{\mathrm{g}} are temperature-dependent [18, 19].

2.1.5 Kane models with different number of orbitals

The Kane model can also be formulated with a different number of orbitals. For example, a simpler 𝟔×𝟔6\times 6 version can be used, where the �𝟕\Gamma_{7} orbitals are omitted. Another version contains 𝟏𝟒14 orbitals, which adds a quadruplet of �𝟖\Gamma_{8} states and a doublet of �𝟕\Gamma_{7} states in the conduction band. We will neither consider the 𝟏𝟒14 orbital in this work nor have implemented it into kdotpy, because the six additional orbitals add complexity that is not necessary for most purposes for which we use kdotpy. The so-called Luttinger model with only the four �𝟖\Gamma_{8} orbitals [20] is also left out of consideration because it cannot capture the essential physics of topological insulators, where �𝟔\Gamma_{6} and �𝟖\Gamma_{8} are inverted.

If one changes perspective between the 𝟔6 and 𝟖8 orbital Kane model, one needs to take into account renormalizations of the coefficients. The reason for this renormalization is that in the 𝟔6 orbital model, the �𝟕\Gamma_{7} orbitals become remote bands, and thus one must consider their additional perturbative contributions 𝐏𝒏′​𝒏\mathbf{P}_{n^{\prime}n} (cf. Eqs. (5) and (6)). This perturbation contributes to (for example) the band masses of the �𝟔\Gamma_{6} and �𝟖\Gamma_{8} orbitals. In the 𝟖8 orbital model, the �𝟕\Gamma_{7} orbitals are treated explicitly and thus its perturbative contribution on the other bands is absent. To ascertain that both models yield the same dispersion, the band masses of the �𝟔\Gamma_{6} and �𝟖\Gamma_{8} orbitals need to be renormalized. Similar renormalizations apply to other coefficients and between different pairs of models. Details are provided, for example, in the tables of Winkler [15].

2.2 Lower dimensional geometries

So far, we have considered the Hamiltonian in terms of the momentum coordinates (𝒌𝒙,𝒌𝒚,𝒌𝒛)(k_{x},k_{y},k_{z}). These momenta are good quantum numbers by virtue of Bloch’s theorem. For Bloch’s theorem to be valid, the system must have (discrete) translational symmetry in three dimensions. Thus, for a bulk crystal, this description is appropriate.

However, experimentally relevant systems are of finite size; thus the translational symmetry is broken. Nevertheless, if the dimensions of the system are sufficiently large, the system may still be treated as approximately infinite. The decisive criterion is the size of the system compared to the de Broglie wavelength of the particles, or equivalently, the (quantum mechanical) confinement energy compared to other energy scales in the system.

Typically, we have a ‘hybrid’ situation, where the system is infinite in some and finite in other directions. For semiconductor devices simulated by kdotpy, we typically consider ‘2D’ and ‘1D’ geometries, where 𝒏nD refers to the number 𝒏n of dimensions in which the system has translational symmetry, or, in other words, the number of momentum coordinates.

A prominent example of a 2D geometry is a quantum well system. In the 2D geometry, translational symmetry is broken in 𝒛z direction whereas it is preserved in the 𝒙x and 𝒚y direction. The appropriate coordinates in this geometry are thus (𝒌𝒙,𝒌𝒚,𝒛)(k_{x},k_{y},z). This system may be thought of as an infinite slab of material. More generically, any stack of layers of different materials, called a ‘layer stack’, is described as a 2D geometry. In this case, the material parameters (like 𝑬𝐜E_{\mathrm{c}}, 𝑬𝐯E_{\mathrm{v}}, 1,2,3, etc.) are treated as a function of 𝒛z 11 1 We treat the Kane parameter PP on equal footing as the other material parameters. In some works (see, e.g., Ref. [2]), it is argued that PP must be equal in all layers, as a result of how it is defined in terms of the atomic orbitals, cf. Eq. (13). Since the model yields physical result also if we relax this restriction, we allow PP to have different values between layers.. The material parameters are effectively constant in the bulk of each layer and transition smoothly between them at the interfaces between layers. Many important topological aspects, like surface states, can exist only at the interface between a topological and a trivial material and thus need to be simulated in the 2D geometry.

The 1D geometry is equivalent to an infinite wire, with translational symmetry only in 𝒙x direction and a finite size both in 𝒚y and 𝒛z direction, with coordinates (𝒌𝒙,𝒚,𝒛)(k_{x},y,z). The extent in 𝒚y and 𝒛z direction must not necessarily be equal or even similar in size. Typically, in order to simulate the edge states of the quantum spin Hall effect, one considers a ‘ribbon’ or ‘strip’ of material, where the thickness is ∼𝟏𝟎​𝐧𝐦\sim 10\,\mathrm{nm} and the width is ∼𝟓𝟎𝟎​𝐧𝐦\sim 500\,\mathrm{nm} or larger [4].

2.2.1 Dimensional reduction

The reduction of the bulk Hamiltonian (3D) to a lower dimensionality is a two step process for each of the confined dimensions. Firstly, the momentum coordinate in the Hamiltonian is substituted by its representation in spatial coordinates. For example, 𝒌𝒛k_{z} is substituted by the derivative −𝐢∂𝒛-\mathrm{i}\partial_{z} (where ∂𝒛=∂/∂𝒛\partial_{z}=\partial/\partial z). Likewise, 𝒌𝒛𝟐k_{z}^{2} is substituted by the second-order derivative −∂𝒛𝟐-\partial_{z}^{2}. These substitutions essentially encode an inverse Fourier transform. Secondly, we choose a finite basis for each spatial direction. This step is necessary, because the computational Hilbert space must be of finite dimension. Here, we specifically choose the basis defined by a finite set of points at which the wave functions are evaluated. We consider uniformly spaced grids of the form {𝒛𝒋}𝒋=𝒋𝐦𝐢𝐧,…,𝒋𝐦𝐚𝐱\{z_{j}\}_{j=j_{\mathrm{min}},\ldots,j_{\mathrm{max}}}, with 𝒛𝒋=𝒋​�​𝒛z_{j}=j\Delta z, where �​𝒛\Delta z is the grid resolution and 𝒋j is an integer index taken from the finite range [𝒋𝐦𝐢𝐧,𝒋𝐦𝐚𝐱][j_{\mathrm{min}},j_{\mathrm{max}}]. We note that our choice differs from the Fortran code of Refs. [2, 3], which uses a set of envelope functions based on Legendre polynomials.

In the chosen basis, the discretization of the first derivatives is given by

2.2.2 Hermitian discretization

In a layered system (2D geometry), where the material parameters are functions of 𝒛z, special care needs to be taken that these functions generally do not commute with 𝒌^𝒛=−𝐢∂𝒛\hat{k}_{z}=-\mathrm{i}\partial_{z}. The operator 𝒌^𝒛\hat{k}_{z} being a derivative, this leads to contributions involving ∂𝒛𝑸\partial_{z}Q. To clarify this statement, it is useful to expand the matrix element ⟨�|{𝑸,𝒌^𝒛}| ⟩\langle\phi|\{Q,\hat{k}_{z}\}|\psi\rangle in terms of its spatial representation as an integral over 𝒛z,

(24)

For the matrix element ⟨�|[𝑸,𝒌^𝒛]| ⟩\langle\phi|[Q,\hat{k}_{z}]|\psi\rangle involving a commutator, we find that

⟨�|[𝑸,𝒌^𝒛]| ⟩=−𝐢∫𝒅𝒛�∗(𝒛)(𝑸(𝒛)∂𝒛−∂𝒛𝑸(𝒛)) (𝒛)=−𝐢∫𝒅𝒛(𝒛)∗𝑸′(𝒛) (𝒛)=⟨�|𝑸′| ⟩.\langle\phi|[Q,\hat{k}_{z}]|\psi\rangle=-\mathrm{i}\int dz\,\phi^{*}(z)\,(Q(z)\partial_{z}-\partial_{z}Q(z))\,\psi(z)=-\mathrm{i}\int dz\,{}^{*}(z)Q^{\prime}(z)\psi(z)=\langle\phi|Q^{\prime}|\psi\rangle. (25)

In other words, the commutator [𝑸,𝒌^𝒛][Q,\hat{k}_{z}] only contributes where 𝑸′​(𝒛)≡∂𝒛𝑸⁡(𝒛)Q^{\prime}(z)\equiv\partial_{z}Q(z) is nonzero, which is only near the interfaces between layers, as the material parameters are constant in the bulk of each layer. The commutator terms can thus be interpreted as interface terms.

On the diagonal of the Hamiltonian, the matrix elements 𝑻𝐤T_{\mathbf{k}} and 𝑼𝐤U_{\mathbf{k}} contain effective-mass terms, quadratic in the momentum 𝒌𝒛k_{z}. The correct substitution to operator form is given by a symmetrized triple product, in general

𝒒​𝒌𝒊​𝒌𝒋→{𝒌𝒊​𝒒​𝒌𝒋}𝐒≡𝟏𝟐​(𝒌^𝒊​𝒒^​𝒌^𝒋+𝒌^𝒋​𝒒^​𝒌^𝒊),qk_{i}k_{j}\to\{k_{i}qk_{j}\}_{\mathrm{S}}\equiv\tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{k}_{i}\hat{q}\hat{k}_{j}+\hat{k}_{j}\hat{q}\hat{k}_{i}), (26)

where 𝒊,𝒋=𝒙,𝒚,𝒛i,j=x,y,z and 𝒒^\hat{q} is a hermitian operator [21, 22, 2]. For the relevant diagonal matrix elements with effective mass terms of the form 𝑸​𝒌𝒛𝟐Qk_{z}^{2}, the substitution rule reads 𝑸​𝒌𝒛𝟐→𝒌^𝒛​𝑸​(𝒛)​𝒌^𝒛Qk_{z}^{2}\to\hat{k}_{z}Q(z)\hat{k}_{z}. In the spatial representation, these terms can be written as

⟨�|𝒌^𝒛𝑸𝒌^𝒛| ⟩=−∫𝒅𝒛�∗(𝒛)∂𝒛(𝑸(𝒛)∂𝒛 (𝒛))=∫𝒅𝒛�′⁣∗(𝒛)𝑸(𝒛)(𝒛)′=⟨�′|𝑸|⟩′,\langle\phi|\hat{k}_{z}Q\hat{k}_{z}|\psi\rangle=-\int dz\,\phi^{*}(z)\partial_{z}(Q(z)\partial_{z}\psi(z))=\int dz\,\phi^{\prime*}(z)Q(z){}^{\prime}(z)=\langle\phi^{\prime}|Q|{}^{\prime}\rangle, (27)

where (𝒛)′≡∂𝒛 (𝒛){}^{\prime}(z)\equiv\partial_{z}\psi(z).

The first-order terms are discretized as follows. We take the form of Eq. (24) and substitute ​(𝒛)→( ​(𝒛+𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛)+ ​(𝒛−𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛))/𝟐\psi(z)\to(\psi(z+\frac{1}{2}\Delta z)+\psi(z-\frac{1}{2}\Delta z))/2 and ∂𝒛 ​(𝒛)→( ​(𝒛+𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛)− ​(𝒛−𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛))/�​𝒛\partial_{z}\psi(z)\to(\psi(z+\frac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\psi(z-\frac{1}{2}\Delta z))/\Delta z and analogous rules for �∗​(𝒛)\phi^{*}(z) and ∂𝒛�∗​(𝒛)\partial_{z}\phi^{*}(z). We thus obtain

−𝐢𝟐​�​𝒛∑𝒛[(�∗(𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)+�∗(𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))𝑸(𝒛)( (𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)− (𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))\displaystyle\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{2\Delta z}\sum_{z}\left[\left(\phi^{*}(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)+\phi^{*}(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right)Q(z)\left(\psi(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\psi(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right)\right.
−(�∗(𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)−�∗(𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))𝑸(𝒛)( (𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)+ (𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))]\displaystyle\hskip 22.99988pt\hskip 22.99988pt-\left.\left(\phi^{*}(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\phi^{*}(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right)Q(z)\left(\psi(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)+\psi(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right)\right] (28)

By expanding and erasing the terms that cancel, we find

−𝐢�​𝒛​∑𝒛(�∗​(𝒛−𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛)​𝑸​(𝒛)​ ​(𝒛+𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛)−�∗​(𝒛+𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛)​𝑸​(𝒛)​ ​(𝒛−𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛))\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{\Delta z}\sum_{z}\left(\phi^{*}(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)Q(z)\psi(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\phi^{*}(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)Q(z)\psi(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right) (29)

In our computational basis, the Hilbert space is defined as the wave functions on the discrete coordinates 𝒛𝒋z_{j}, so we must align 𝒛±𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛z\pm\frac{1}{2}\Delta z with these values. This implies that 𝑸⁡(𝒛)Q(z) is evaluated at intermediate points 𝒛𝒋±𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛z_{j}\pm\frac{1}{2}\Delta z, which is not a problem since 𝑸Q is a function which we can evaluate anywhere. The resulting expression can be written in three equivalent forms, related by shifts of the ‘dummy variable’ 𝒋j,

⟨�|{𝑸,𝒌^𝒛}| ⟩\displaystyle\langle\phi|\{Q,\hat{k}_{z}\}|\psi\rangle →−𝐢�​𝒛∑𝒋(�𝒋∗𝑸(𝒛𝒋+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)−𝒋+𝟏�𝒋∗𝑸(𝒛𝒋−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))𝒋−𝟏\displaystyle\to\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{\Delta z}\sum_{j}\left(\phi^{*}_{j}\,Q(z_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\,{}_{j+1}-\phi^{*}_{j}\,Q(z_{j}-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\,{}_{j-1}\right) (30)
=−𝐢�​𝒛∑𝒋𝑸(𝒛𝒋−𝟏𝟐�𝒛)(�𝒋−𝟏∗−𝒋�𝒋∗)𝒋−𝟏\displaystyle=\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{\Delta z}\sum_{j}Q(z_{j}-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\left(\phi^{*}_{j-1}\,{}_{j}-\phi^{*}_{j}\,{}_{j-1}\right) (31)
=−𝐢�​𝒛∑𝒋𝑸(𝒛𝒋+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)(�𝒋∗−𝒋+𝟏�𝒋+𝟏∗)𝒋.\displaystyle=\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{\Delta z}\sum_{j}Q(z_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\left(\phi^{*}_{j}\,{}_{j+1}-\phi^{*}_{j+1}\,{}_{j}\right). (32)

We use the first form [Eq. (30)] to extract the action of the Hamiltonian matrix, (𝑯 )𝒊=∑𝒋𝑯𝒊​𝒋𝒋(H\psi)_{i}=\sum_{j}H_{ij}{}_{j}. From the second and third forms [Eqs. (31) and (32)], we find that the resulting Hamiltonian matrix is hermitian.

For the matrix elements of commutator form [𝑸,𝒌^𝒛][Q,\hat{k}_{z}], we simply substitute the derivative 𝑸′Q^{\prime} into Eq. (25),

⟨�|[𝑸,𝒌^𝒛]| ⟩→∑𝒋�𝒋∗𝑸′(𝒛𝒋),𝒋\langle\phi|[Q,\hat{k}_{z}]|\psi\rangle\to\sum_{j}\phi^{*}_{j}Q^{\prime}(z_{j}){}_{j}, (33)

where 𝑸′​(𝒛𝒋)Q^{\prime}(z_{j}) is the derivative of 𝑸Q evaluated at the grid point 𝒛𝒋z_{j}. In kdotpy, we use the discrete derivative 𝑸′​(𝒛𝒋)=(𝑸′​(𝒛𝒋+�​𝒛)−𝑸′​(𝒛𝒋−�​𝒛))/𝟐​�​𝒛Q^{\prime}(z_{j})=(Q^{\prime}(z_{j}+\Delta z)-Q^{\prime}(z_{j}-\Delta z))/2\Delta z.

The discretization of the quadratic terms follows from Eq. (27), where we substitute (𝒛)′=∂𝒛 (𝒛)→( (𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)− (𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))/�𝒛{}^{\prime}(z)=\partial_{z}\psi(z)\to(\psi(z+\frac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\psi(z-\frac{1}{2}\Delta z))/\Delta z. We thus obtain

−𝟏�​𝒛𝟐∑𝒛(�∗(𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)−�∗(𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛))𝑸(𝒛)( (𝒛+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)− (𝒛−𝟏𝟐�𝒛)).-\frac{1}{\Delta z^{2}}\sum_{z}\left(\phi^{*}(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\phi^{*}(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right)Q(z)\left(\psi(z+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)-\psi(z-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\right). (34)

We expand and align 𝒛±𝟏𝟐​�​𝒛z\pm\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z with the discrete coordinates 𝒛𝒋z_{j}, and obtain

⟨�|𝒌^𝒛​𝑸​𝒌^𝒛| ⟩\displaystyle\langle\phi|\hat{k}_{z}Q\hat{k}_{z}|\psi\rangle →𝟏�​𝒛𝟐∑𝒋(�𝒋∗𝑸(𝒛𝒋+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)(−𝒋+𝟏)𝒋+�𝒋∗𝑸(𝒛𝒋−𝟏𝟐�𝒛)(−𝒋−𝟏)𝒋)\displaystyle\to\frac{1}{\Delta z^{2}}\sum_{j}\left(\phi^{*}_{j}\,Q(z_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\,({}_{j+1}-{}_{j})+\phi^{*}_{j}\,Q(z_{j}-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\,({}_{j-1}-{}_{j})\right) (35)
=−𝟏�​𝒛𝟐∑𝒋(�𝒋∗−�𝒋−𝟏∗)𝑸(𝒛𝒋−𝟏𝟐�𝒛)(−𝒋)𝒋−𝟏\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\Delta z^{2}}\sum_{j}(\phi^{*}_{j}-\phi^{*}_{j-1})\,Q(z_{j}-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\,({}_{j}-{}_{j-1}) (36)
=−𝟏�​𝒛𝟐∑𝒋(�𝒋+𝟏∗−�𝒋∗)𝑸(𝒛𝒋+𝟏𝟐�𝒛)(−𝒋+𝟏)𝒋.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\Delta z^{2}}\sum_{j}(\phi^{*}_{j+1}-\phi^{*}_{j})\,Q(z_{j}+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta z)\,({}_{j+1}-{}_{j}). (37)

The first form [Eq. (35)] again defines the action of the Hamiltonian matrix (𝑯 )𝒊=∑𝒋𝑯𝒊​𝒋𝒋(H\psi)_{i}=\sum_{j}H_{ij}{}_{j} and the second and third forms [Eqs. (36) and (37)] show that the expression is hermitian if =�\psi=\phi.

2.3 Magnetic fields

2.3.1 Peierls substitution

In (classical) Hamiltonian mechanics, the motion of a charged particle with dispersion 𝒑𝟐/𝟐​𝒎p^{2}/2m and charge −𝒆-e in a magnetic field 𝐁\mathbf{B} is given by

𝑯=𝟏𝟐​𝒎​(𝐩+𝒆​𝐀)𝟐,H=\frac{1}{2m}\left(\mathbf{p}+e\mathbf{A}\right)^{2}, (38)

in terms of the magnetic gauge field 𝐀\mathbf{A} that satisfies 𝐁=∇×𝐀\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}. In this expression, 𝐩\mathbf{p} acts as the canonical momentum, while �=𝐩+𝒆​𝐀\mathbf{\Pi}=\mathbf{p}+e\mathbf{A} is the kinetic momentum, equal to mass times velocity. In order to obtain the Hamiltonian for the motion of a particle in a magnetic field from a generic zero-field Hamiltonian, one applies the Peierls substitution

𝐩→�=𝐩+𝒆​𝐀,\mathbf{p}\to\mathbf{\Pi}=\mathbf{p}+e\mathbf{A}, (39)

or equivalently, 𝐤→𝐤+(𝒆/˜​𝒉)​𝐀\mathbf{k}\to\mathbf{k}+(e/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})\mathbf{A}.

The electromagnetic gauge field 𝐀\mathbf{A} is subject to gauge invariance by the transformation 𝐀→𝐀+∇�\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{A}+\nabla\Lambda where �\Lambda is a function depending on the spatial coordinates. This gauge transformation does not alter the relation 𝐁=∇×𝐀\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}. (Here, and in the remainder of the work, we assume that 𝐁\mathbf{B} and 𝐀\mathbf{A} are not time-dependent.) This leaves us with a freedom to choose the gauge conveniently. For example, for a perpendicular magnetic field 𝐁=(𝟎,𝟎,𝑩𝒛)\mathbf{B}=(0,0,B_{z}), two common gauge choices are the symmetric gauge 𝐀=𝑩𝒛(−𝒚/𝟐,𝒙/𝟐,𝟎)\mathbf{A}=B_{z}(-y/2,x/2,0) and the Lorentz gauge 𝐀=𝑩𝒛​(−𝒚,𝟎,𝟎)\mathbf{A}=B_{z}(-y,0,0). For the numerical simulations, one should notice that the symmetric gauge breaks translational invariance in 𝒙x and 𝒚y direction, while the Lorentz gauge breaks it in 𝒚y direction only. Thus, for simulations of a device in a magnetic field, kdotpy uses the Lorentz gauge so that the translational symmetry in 𝒙x direction is left intact. This simulation is done in the strip geometry, i.e., the 1D geometry with momentum coordinates 𝒌𝒙k_{x} and spatial coordinates 𝒚y and 𝒛z.

For in-plane fields 𝐁=(𝑩𝒙,𝑩𝒚,𝟎)\mathbf{B}=(B_{x},B_{y},0), on similar grounds we choose a gauge that depends only on the 𝒛z coordinate, leaving translational symmetries in 𝒙x and 𝒚y directions intact (if they are not yet broken by some other means). The gauge that satisfies this property is 𝐀=(𝑩𝒚​𝒛,−𝑩𝒙​𝒛,𝟎)\mathbf{A}=(B_{y}z,-B_{x}z,0). For generic magnetic fields 𝐁=(𝑩𝒙,𝑩𝒚,𝑩𝒛)\mathbf{B}=(B_{x},B_{y},B_{z}) we simply take the sum of in-plane and out-of-plane, and use the gauge

𝐀=(𝑩𝒚​𝒛−𝑩𝒛​𝒚,−𝑩𝒙​𝒛,𝟎).\mathbf{A}=(B_{y}z-B_{z}y,-B_{x}z,0). (40)

The appropriate geometry for the simulations depends on the out-of-plane component: If 𝑩𝒛≠𝟎B_{z}\not=0, a 1D geometry is needed, while for a purely in-plane field, the 2D geometry is typically the appropriate one.

In quantum mechanics, the momentum and gauge fields discussed above must be replaced by the appropriate operators. Importantly, the momentum 𝒌^\hat{k} and gauge field 𝑨^\hat{A} operators (which is a function of spatial coordinates) do not commute in general. We quantize the quadratic terms in a symmetric way

(𝒌𝒊+𝒆˜​𝒉​𝑨𝒊)​(𝒌𝒋+𝒆˜​𝒉​𝑨𝒋)\displaystyle\left(k_{i}+\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}A_{i}\right)\left(k_{j}+\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}A_{j}\right) →𝒌^𝒊​𝒌^𝒋+𝒆˜​𝒉​(𝒌^𝒊​𝑨𝒋+𝒌^𝒋​𝑨𝒊)+(𝒆˜​𝒉)𝟐​𝑨𝒊​𝑨𝒋\displaystyle\to\hat{k}_{i}\hat{k}_{j}+\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}(\hat{k}_{i}A_{j}+\hat{k}_{j}A_{i})+\left(\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}\right)^{2}A_{i}A_{j} (41)
=−∂𝒊∂𝒋−𝐢𝒆˜​𝒉(∂𝒊𝑨𝒋+∂𝒋𝑨𝒊+𝑨𝒊∂𝒋+𝑨𝒋∂𝒊)+(𝒆˜​𝒉)𝟐𝑨𝒊𝑨𝒋\displaystyle=-\partial_{i}\partial_{j}-\mathrm{i}\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}\left(\partial_{i}A_{j}+\partial_{j}A_{i}+A_{i}\partial_{j}+A_{j}\partial_{i}\right)+\left(\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}\right)^{2}A_{i}A_{j} (42)

with 𝒊,𝒋=𝒙,𝒚,𝒛i,j=x,y,z, because this form assures that the Hamiltonian is hermitian [23]. The Hamiltonian is gauge invariant under the gauge transformation 𝐀→𝐀+∇�\mathbf{A}\to\mathbf{A}+\nabla\Lambda and | ⟩→𝐞𝐱𝐩(−𝐢𝒆�/˜​𝒉)| ⟩\lvert\psi\rangle\to\exp(-\mathrm{i}e\Lambda/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})\lvert\psi\rangle, where �\Lambda is a function of the spatial coordinates [23].

Importantly, the kinetic momentum operators do not commute,

[𝒌𝒊+𝒆˜​𝒉𝑨𝒊,𝒌𝒋+𝒆˜​𝒉𝑨𝒋]=−𝐢𝒆˜​𝒉(∂𝒊𝑨𝒋−∂𝒋𝑨𝒊)=−𝐢𝒆˜​𝒉∑𝒌�𝒊​𝒋​𝒌𝑩𝒌,\left[k_{i}+\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}A_{i},k_{j}+\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}A_{j}\right]=-\mathrm{i}\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}(\partial_{i}A_{j}-\partial_{j}A_{i})=-\mathrm{i}\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}\sum_{k}\epsilon_{ijk}B_{k}, (43)

which raises the question how terms of the form (𝒌𝒊+(𝒆/˜​𝒉)​𝑨𝒊)​(𝒌𝒋+(𝒆/˜​𝒉)​𝑨𝒋)(k_{i}+(e/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})A_{i})(k_{j}+(e/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})A_{j}) should be quantized. Obviously, if 𝒊=𝒋i=j, there is no ambiguity. For the off-diagonal terms, we assume the following quantization rules

𝒌±𝟐\displaystyle k_{\pm}^{2} →(𝒌^𝒙′)𝟐−(𝒌^𝒚′)𝟐±𝐢⁡(𝒌^𝒙′​𝒌^𝒚′+𝒌^𝒚′​𝒌^𝒙′)\displaystyle\to(\hat{k}^{\prime}_{x})^{2}-(\hat{k}^{\prime}_{y})^{2}\pm\mathrm{i}(\hat{k}^{\prime}_{x}\hat{k}^{\prime}_{y}+\hat{k}^{\prime}_{y}\hat{k}^{\prime}_{x})
=−∂𝒙𝟐+∂𝒚𝟐∓𝟐𝐢∂𝒙∂𝒚+𝟐𝒆˜​𝒉(𝑨𝒙±𝐢𝑨𝒚)(−𝐢∂𝒙±∂𝒚)∓𝒆˜​𝒉𝑩𝒛+(𝒆˜​𝒉)𝟐(𝑨𝒙±𝐢𝑨𝒚)𝟐\displaystyle=-\partial_{x}^{2}+\partial_{y}^{2}\mp 2\mathrm{i}\partial_{x}\partial_{y}+2\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}(A_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}A_{y})(-\mathrm{i}\partial_{x}\pm\partial_{y})\mp\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}B_{z}+\left(\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}\right)^{2}(A_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}A_{y})^{2} (44)
𝒌±​𝒌𝒛\displaystyle k_{\pm}k_{z} →𝟏𝟐​{𝒌^𝒙′±𝐢​𝒌^𝒚′,𝒌^𝒛′}\displaystyle\to\tfrac{1}{2}\{\hat{k}^{\prime}_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}\hat{k}^{\prime}_{y},\hat{k}^{\prime}_{z}\}
=−𝐢(∂𝒙±𝐢∂𝒚)∂𝒛−𝐢𝒆˜​𝒉(𝑨𝒙±𝐢𝑨𝒚)∂𝒛∓𝒆𝟐​˜​𝒉(𝑩𝒙±𝐢𝑩𝒚)\displaystyle=-\mathrm{i}(\partial_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}\partial_{y})\partial_{z}-\mathrm{i}\frac{e}{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}(A_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}A_{y})\partial_{z}\mp\frac{e}{2\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}(B_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}B_{y}) (45)

where we have defined 𝒌^𝒊′=𝒌^+(𝒆/˜​𝒉)​𝑨𝒊\hat{k}^{\prime}_{i}=\hat{k}+(e/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})A_{i} and we have assumed the gauge defined by Eq. (40). The terms 𝒆​𝑩𝒛/˜​𝒉eB_{z}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h} and 𝒆⁡(𝑩𝒙±𝐢​𝑩𝒚)/𝟐​˜​𝒉e(B_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}B_{y})/2\mathord{\mathchar 126h} in Eqs. (44) and (45), respectively, can be interpreted as originating from the non-commutative character of the kinetic momentum operators. For the sake of doing the numerics, we further substitute 𝑨𝒙±𝐢​𝑨𝒚=(𝑩𝒚∓𝐢​𝑩𝒙)​𝒛−𝑩𝒛​𝒚=∓𝐢⁡(𝑩𝒙±𝐢​𝑩𝒚)​𝒛−𝑩𝒛​𝒚A_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}A_{y}=(B_{y}\mp\mathrm{i}B_{x})z-B_{z}y=\mp\mathrm{i}(B_{x}\pm\mathrm{i}B_{y})z-B_{z}y.

2.3.2 Out-of-plane magnetic field in strip geometry

The case of a pure out-of-plane field, 𝐁=(𝟎,𝟎,𝑩𝒛)\mathbf{B}=(0,0,B_{z}), can be treated in the strip geometry, i.e., the 1D case with coordinates (𝒌𝒙,𝒚,𝒛)(k_{x},y,z). We choose the gauge 𝐀=(𝑨𝒙,𝟎,𝟎)\mathbf{A}=(A_{x},0,0) with 𝑨𝒙=−𝑩𝒛​(𝒚−𝒚𝟎)A_{x}=-B_{z}(y-y_{0}), where the gauge origin 𝒚𝟎y_{0} can be freely chosen.

In kdotpy, we choose 𝒚𝟎=𝟎y_{0}=0 to be the centre of the strip, so that 𝑨𝒙A_{x} is antisymmetric under reflection in 𝒚y. The momentum coordinate is simply shifted according to the Peierls substitution, 𝒌𝒙→𝒌𝒙−(𝒆/˜​𝒉)​𝑩𝒛​𝒚k_{x}\to k_{x}-(e/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})B_{z}y. 2.3.4 Generic magnetic fields

For a generic magnetic field 𝐁=(𝑩𝒙,𝑩𝒚,𝑩𝒛)\mathbf{B}=(B_{x},B_{y},B_{z}), we can straightforwardly adapt the equations above. For the 𝒌±𝟐k_{\pm}^{2} terms, we simply make the substitutions 𝒌^𝒙′=𝒌𝒙−(𝒆​𝑩𝒛/˜​𝒉)​𝒚+(𝒆​𝑩𝒚/˜​𝒉)​𝒛\hat{k}^{\prime}_{x}=k_{x}-(eB_{z}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})y+(eB_{y}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})z and 𝒌^𝒚′=−𝐢∂𝒚−(𝒆𝑩𝒙/˜​𝒉)𝒛\hat{k}^{\prime}_{y}=-\mathrm{i}\partial_{y}-(eB_{x}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})z, adding the in-plane component of the field to the gauge compared to Eq. (44). The derivative ∂𝒚\partial_{y} commutes with the terms proportional with 𝒛z, hence no extra terms of the form 𝒆​𝑩𝒙/˜​𝒉eB_{x}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h} or 𝒆​𝑩𝒚/˜​𝒉eB_{y}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h} (constant in space) appear. Likewise, for 𝒌±′{,𝟑𝒌^𝒛}k^{\prime}_{\pm}\{{}_{3},\hat{k}_{z}\}, the out-of-plane component appears as an extra term (𝒆​𝑩𝒛/˜​𝒉)​𝒚(eB_{z}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})y in 𝒌𝒙+(𝒆/˜​𝒉)​𝑨𝒙k_{x}+(e/\mathord{\mathchar 126h})A_{x} compared to Eqs. (49) and (50). This term commutes with ∂𝒛\partial_{z}.

2.4 Landau level formalism

2.4.1 Out-of-plane field in the axial approximation

If the magnetic field is purely out-of-plane, we have the commutator relation [𝒌^−′,𝒌^+′]=𝟐​𝒆​𝑩𝒛/˜​𝒉[\hat{k}^{\prime}_{-},\hat{k}^{\prime}_{+}]=2eB_{z}/\mathord{\mathchar 126h} while 𝒌^𝒛′\hat{k}^{\prime}_{z} commutes with both 𝒌^𝒙′\hat{k}^{\prime}_{x} and 𝒌^𝒚′\hat{k}^{\prime}_{y}. This structure is formally equivalent to the ladder operators of the harmonic oscillator with commutation relation [𝒂,𝒂†]=𝟏[a,a^{\dagger}]=1, if we define

𝒂=˜​𝒉𝟐​𝒆​𝑩𝒛​𝒌^−′=𝟏𝟐​𝒍𝑩​𝒌^−′,𝒂†=˜​𝒉𝟐​𝒆​𝑩𝒛​𝒌+′=𝟏𝟐​𝒍𝑩​𝒌^+′,a=\sqrt{\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{2eB_{z}}}\hat{k}^{\prime}_{-}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}l_{B}\hat{k}^{\prime}_{-},\hskip 22.99988pta^{\dagger}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}}{2eB_{z}}}k^{\prime}_{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}l_{B}\hat{k}^{\prime}_{+}, (51)

where 𝒍𝑩=˜​𝒉/𝒆​𝑩𝒛l_{B}=\sqrt{\mathord{\mathchar 126h}/eB_{z}} is the magnetic length. (Here, we have tacitly assumed 𝑩𝒛>𝟎B_{z}>0.) The eigenstates of the number operator 𝒂†​𝒂a^{\dagger}a are denoted |𝒏⟩\lvert n\rangle, where 𝒏n is the eigenvalue, i.e., 𝒂†𝒂|𝒏⟩=𝒏|𝒏⟩a^{\dagger}a\lvert n\rangle=n\lvert n\rangle. The raising and lowering operator act as 𝒂†|𝒏⟩=𝒏+𝟏|𝒏+𝟏⟩a^{\dagger}\lvert n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}\lvert n+1\rangle and 𝒂|𝒏⟩=𝒏−𝟏|𝒏−𝟏⟩a\lvert n\rangle=\sqrt{n-1}\lvert n-1\rangle, respectively.

In this context, these eigenstates are called Landau level states (see, e.g., Refs. [2, 3]). The Hamiltonian can be reformulated in terms of ladder operators by substituting 𝒌+k_{+} and 𝒌−k_{-} by 𝒂†a^{\dagger} and 𝒂a, respectively. The combination 𝒌𝒙𝟐+𝒌𝒚𝟐=𝟏𝟐​(𝒌+​𝒌−+𝒌−​𝒌+)k_{x}^{2}+k_{y}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}(k_{+}k_{-}+k_{-}k_{+}) is substituted by a term proportional to 𝒂†​𝒂+𝒂​𝒂†=𝟐​𝒏+𝟏a^{\dagger}a+aa^{\dagger}=2n+1.

It can be shown [2, 3] that in the axial approximation, the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian can be written in the form

|⟩(𝒏)=(𝒇(𝒏)𝟏(𝒛)|𝒏⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟐(𝒛)|𝒏+𝟏⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟑(𝒛)|𝒏−𝟏⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟒(𝒛)|𝒏⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟓(𝒛)|𝒏+𝟏⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟔(𝒛)|𝒏+𝟐⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟕(𝒛)|𝒏⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟖(𝒛)|𝒏+𝟏⟩),\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}f^{(n)}_{1}(z)\lvert n\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{2}(z)\lvert n+1\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{3}(z)\lvert n-1\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{4}(z)\lvert n\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{5}(z)\lvert n+1\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{6}(z)\lvert n+2\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{7}(z)\lvert n\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{8}(z)\lvert n+1\rangle\end{pmatrix}, (52)

where 𝒏=−𝟐,−𝟏,𝟎,𝟏,…n=-2,-1,0,1,\ldots is called the Landau level index (LL index). For 𝒏=−𝟐,−𝟏,𝟎n=-2,-1,0, some of the indices 𝒏′n^{\prime} in |𝒏′⟩\lvert n^{\prime}\rangle on the right-hand side are negative; these components are understood to be zero. For 𝒏≥𝟏n\geq 1, the dimension of the subspace spanned by |⟩(𝒏)\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle is 𝟖​𝒏𝒛8n_{z}, where 𝒏𝒛n_{z} is the number of degrees of freedom in the 𝒛z direction. (For discrete coordinates 𝒛𝒋z_{j}, as in the kdotpy calculation, 𝒏𝒛n_{z} is equal to the number of grid points.) For 𝒏=−𝟐,−𝟏,𝟎n=-2,-1,0, the dimensionality of the subspace is reduced to 𝟏​𝒏𝒛1n_{z}, 𝟒​𝒏𝒛4n_{z}, and 𝟕​𝒏𝒛7n_{z}, respectively, where 𝟏1, 𝟒4, and 𝟕7 refer to the number of nonzero components in Eq. (52). This observation is important for the implementation, as we will discuss in detail later.

The Landau level index 𝒏n is a conserved quantity in axial approximation [where we neglect 𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱R^{\mathrm{nonax}}_{\mathbf{k}}, Eq. (17)], meaning that the Hamiltonian is block-diagonal in the basis {|⟩(𝒏)}𝒏=−𝟐,−𝟏,𝟎,𝟏,…\{\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle\}_{n=-2,-1,0,1,\ldots}, i.e., ⟨�(𝒏′)|𝑯𝐚𝐱|⟩(𝒏)=𝟎\langle\Phi^{(n^{\prime})}|H^{\mathrm{ax}}|{}^{(n)}\rangle=0 if 𝒏′≠𝒏n^{\prime}\neq n. This property allows to calculate Landau level spectra separately for each Landau level 𝒏=−𝟐,−𝟏,𝟎,…,𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n=-2,-1,0,\ldots,n_{\mathrm{max}}, where 𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n_{\mathrm{max}} is the desired maximal Landau level index. The result is a set of magnetic-field dependent energy eigenvalues 𝑬𝒋(𝒏)​(𝑩𝒛)E^{(n)}_{j}(B_{z}) for each Landau index 𝒏n, where 𝒋j runs over all eigenstates within each Landau level. Due to the fact that the basis is finite, by choosing a Landau level cutoff 𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n_{\mathrm{max}}, the spectrum is inherently incomplete. This is typically a problem only at small magnetic fields, where the energy spacing between Landau levels is small. This energy spacing is equivalent to the cyclotron energy ˜​𝒉​!𝒄=˜​𝒉​𝒆​𝑩𝒛/𝒎\mathord{\mathchar 126h}\omega_{c}=\mathord{\mathchar 126h}eB_{z}/m known from the theory of the quantum Hall effect.

2.4.2 Landau level formalism with axial symmetry breaking

If the nonaxial term 𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}} [Eq. (17)] is added, the Landau level index is no longer a conserved quantum number. In order to demonstrate this, let us define

𝑯𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱=𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱(|𝟑⟩⟨𝟓|+|𝟒⟩⟨𝟔|)+𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱†(|𝟓⟩⟨𝟑|+|𝟔⟩⟨𝟒|)H^{\mathrm{nonax}}=R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}}(\lvert\mathbf{3}\rangle\langle\mathbf{5}\rvert+\lvert\mathbf{4}\rangle\langle\mathbf{6}\rvert)+R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}\dagger}(\lvert\mathbf{5}\rangle\langle\mathbf{3}\rvert+\lvert\mathbf{6}\rangle\langle\mathbf{4}\rvert) (53)

to be the nonaxial part of the Hamiltonian, expressed in the orbital basis of Eq. (10) (with bold-face numbers indicating the orbitals). In the ladder operator formalism, 𝑹𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱∼𝒂†​𝒂†R_{\mathbf{k}}^{\mathrm{nonax}}\sim a^{\dagger}a^{\dagger}, so that

𝑯𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱|⟩(𝒏)∼[(|𝟑⟩⟨𝟓|+|𝟒⟩⟨𝟔|)𝒂†𝒂†+(|𝟓⟩⟨𝟑|+|𝟔⟩⟨𝟒|)𝒂𝒂]|⟩(𝒏)∼(𝟎𝟎𝒇(𝒏)𝟓(𝒛)𝒏+𝟐𝒏+𝟑|𝒏+𝟑⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟔(𝒛)𝒏+𝟐𝒏+𝟑|𝒏+𝟒⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟑(𝒛)𝒏−𝟏𝒏−𝟐|𝒏−𝟑⟩𝒇(𝒏)𝟒(𝒛)𝒏𝒏−𝟏|𝒏−𝟐⟩𝟎𝟎),H^{\mathrm{nonax}}\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle\sim[(\lvert\mathbf{3}\rangle\langle\mathbf{5}\rvert+\lvert\mathbf{4}\rangle\langle\mathbf{6}\rvert)a^{\dagger}a^{\dagger}+(\lvert\mathbf{5}\rangle\langle\mathbf{3}\rvert+\lvert\mathbf{6}\rangle\langle\mathbf{4}\rvert)aa]\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle\sim\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\\ f^{(n)}_{5}(z)\sqrt{n+2}\sqrt{n+3}\lvert n+3\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{6}(z)\sqrt{n+2}\sqrt{n+3}\lvert n+4\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{3}(z)\sqrt{n-1}\sqrt{n-2}\lvert n-3\rangle\\ f^{(n)}_{4}(z)\sqrt{n}\sqrt{n-1}\lvert n-2\rangle\\ 0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, (54)

where ∼\sim indicates that we have suppressed the prefactors in the notation. Examining Eqs. (52) and (54), we observe that ⟨�(𝒏′)|𝑯𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱|⟩(𝒏)\langle\Phi^{(n^{\prime})}|H^{\mathrm{nonax}}|{}^{(n)}\rangle is generally nonzero if 𝒏′=𝒏±𝟒n^{\prime}=n\pm 4 and zero otherwise. Thus, the nonaxial terms couple Landau levels with indices differing by 𝟒4. In the basis of |⟩(𝒏)\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle, the total Hamiltonian (axial and nonaxial terms) has matrix elements between the 𝒏n and 𝒏′n^{\prime} blocks for 𝒏′−𝒏=−𝟒,𝟎,𝟒n^{\prime}-n=-4,0,4. We note that the Landau index modulo 𝟒4 remains conserved, because ⟨�(𝒏′)|𝑯𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐱|⟩(𝒏)=𝟎\langle\Phi^{(n^{\prime})}|H^{\mathrm{nonax}}|{}^{(n)}\rangle=0 if 𝒏′−𝒏n^{\prime}-n is not divisable by 𝟒4.

The block off-diagonal (𝒏′≠𝒏n^{\prime}\neq n) nonaxial terms are typically much weaker than dominant axial terms on the block diagonal (𝒏′=𝒏n^{\prime}=n), so that the former can be viewed as perturbation to the latter. For this reason, basis of Landau level states is still useful even if the Landau index is not conserved. In typical Landau level spectra, the Landau index is often almost conserved, unless two levels of indices 𝒏n, 𝒏′n^{\prime} with 𝒏′−𝒏=±𝟒n^{\prime}-n=\pm 4 come close in energy: In the latter case, hybridization between the states occurs and the spectrum exhibits an anticrossing.

In kdotpy, we always use the Landau level basis in the Landau level mode (kdotpy ll). In the axial approximation where the Hamiltonian matrix is block diagonal, the diagonalization can thus be performed block by block, which gives a performance bonus in view of the smaller matrix size. If nonaxial terms are considered, the Hamiltonian is written as one large matrix with all |⟩(𝒏)\lvert{}^{(n)}\rangle with 𝒏=−𝟐,−𝟏,𝟎,…,𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n=-2,-1,0,\ldots,n_{\mathrm{max}}. This Hamiltonian is diagonalized as a whole. In kdotpy, we do not perform perturbation theory explicitly, but always diagonalize the full matrix. Due to the upper limit 𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n_{\mathrm{max}}, the levels with 𝒏=𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱−𝟑,𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱−𝟐,𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱−𝟏,𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n=n_{\mathrm{max}}-3,n_{\mathrm{max}}-2,n_{\mathrm{max}}-1,n_{\mathrm{max}} are not coupled to their counterpart with 𝒏′=𝒏+𝟒n^{\prime}=n+4; as a result, there is a slight inaccuracy in the energies of the highest levels. This numerical error can often be estimated by raising 𝒏𝐦𝐚𝐱n_{\mathrm{max}} and analyzing how well the energies have converged to definite value.

2.5 Other magnetic couplings

2.5.1 Zeeman effect

The electrons are subject to additional magnetic coupling, for example the Zeeman effect 𝑯𝐙=𝒈​�𝑩​𝐁⋅𝐒H_{\mathrm{Z}}=g\mu_{B}\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{S}, where 𝒈g is the gyromagnetic ratio or “𝒈g-factor” (𝒈≈𝟐g\approx 2 in vacuum), �𝑩\mu_{B} is the Bohr magneton, and 𝐒\mathbf{S} is the vector of spin operators (𝑺^𝒙,𝑺^𝒚,𝑺^𝒛)(\hat{S}_{x},\hat{S}_{y},\hat{S}_{z}). The nonzero blocks (cf. Eq. (12)) of the Zeeman Hamiltonian 𝑯𝒁H_{Z} are

𝑯𝐙,𝟔𝟔\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{Z,66}} =𝒈𝐞​�𝑩​(𝟏𝟐​𝑩𝒛𝟏𝟐​𝑩−𝟏𝟐​𝑩+−𝟏𝟐​𝑩𝒛),\displaystyle=g_{\mathrm{e}}\mu_{B}\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1}{2}B_{z}&\tfrac{1}{2}B_{-}\\ \tfrac{1}{2}B_{+}&-\tfrac{1}{2}B_{z}\end{pmatrix}, 𝑯𝐙,𝟖𝟖\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{Z,88}} =𝟐​�​�𝑩​(−𝟑𝟐​𝑩𝒛−𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝑩−𝟎𝟎−𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝑩+−𝟏𝟐​𝑩𝒛−𝑩−𝟎𝟎−𝑩+𝟏𝟐​𝑩𝒛−𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝑩−𝟎𝟎−𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝑩+𝟑𝟐​𝑩𝒛)\displaystyle=2\kappa\mu_{B}\begin{pmatrix}-\tfrac{3}{2}B_{z}&-\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}B_{-}&0&0\\ -\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}B_{+}&-\tfrac{1}{2}B_{z}&-B_{-}&0\\ 0&-B_{+}&\tfrac{1}{2}B_{z}&-\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}B_{-}\\ 0&0&-\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}B_{+}&\tfrac{3}{2}B_{z}\end{pmatrix}
𝑯𝐙,𝟕𝟕\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{Z,77}} =𝟐​(�+𝟏𝟐)​�𝑩​(−𝟏𝟐​𝑩𝒛−𝟏𝟐​𝑩−−𝟏𝟐​𝑩+𝟏𝟐​𝑩𝒛),\displaystyle=2(\kappa+\tfrac{1}{2})\mu_{B}\begin{pmatrix}-\tfrac{1}{2}B_{z}&-\tfrac{1}{2}B_{-}\\ -\tfrac{1}{2}B_{+}&\tfrac{1}{2}B_{z}\end{pmatrix}, 𝑯𝐙,𝟖𝟕\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{Z,87}} =𝟐​(�+𝟏)​�𝑩​(𝟑/𝟖​𝑩−𝟎−𝟏/𝟐​𝑩𝒛𝟏/𝟖​𝑩−−𝟏/𝟖​𝑩+−𝟏/𝟐​𝑩𝒛𝟎−𝟑/𝟖​𝑩+)\displaystyle=2(\kappa+1)\mu_{B}\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{3/8}B_{-}&0\\ -\sqrt{1/2}B_{z}&\sqrt{1/8}B_{-}\\ -\sqrt{1/8}B_{+}&-\sqrt{1/2}B_{z}\\ 0&-\sqrt{3/8}B_{+}\end{pmatrix} (55)

where 𝒈𝒆g_{e} is the 𝒈g-factor for the �𝟔\Gamma_{6} block and −𝟐​�-2\kappa acts as the 𝒈g-factor of the combined �𝟖,�𝟕\Gamma_{8},\Gamma_{7} block [2, 3, 15].

2.5.2 Exchange coupling in Mn-doped materials

In the dilute magnetic semiconductor Hg1-yMnyTe, the Mn atoms carry a finite magnetic moment, such that the material behaves paramagnetically if the Mn content 𝒚y does not exceed a few percent [24]. The coupling between the Mn magnetic moments and the carrier spins has a similar matrix structure as the Zeeman effect [Eq. (55)], but the response to the external magnetic field 𝐁\mathbf{B} is nonlinear. This coupling is modelled by the (paramagnetic) exchange Hamiltonian [24, 3, 4],

𝑯𝐞𝐱=∑𝒍𝑪(𝒍)​⟨𝐦⟩⋅𝐒(𝒍),H_{\mathrm{ex}}=\sum_{l}C^{(l)}\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle\cdot\mathbf{S}^{(l)}, (56)

where 𝒍l labels the blocks, (the �𝟔\Gamma_{6} block and the �𝟖,�𝟕\Gamma_{8},\Gamma_{7} block), ⟨𝐦⟩\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle is the average Mn spin and 𝐒(𝒍)\mathbf{S}^{(l)} the spin operators of the respective block. The coupling constants 𝑪(𝒍)C^{(l)} (cf. 𝒈𝒆g_{e} and 𝟐​�2\kappa in Eq. (55)) are phenomenologically determined material parameters. For Hg1-yMnyTe, we assume that they are proportional to the Mn content 𝒚y,

𝑪�𝟔=−𝒚​𝑵𝟎​�and𝑪�𝟖,�𝟕=−𝒚​𝑵𝟎​�,C^{\Gamma_{6}}=-yN_{0}\alpha\hskip 22.99988pt\text{and}\hskip 22.99988ptC^{\Gamma_{8},\Gamma_{7}}=-yN_{0}\beta, (57)

with 𝑵𝟎​�=𝟒𝟎𝟎​𝐦𝐞𝐕N_{0}\alpha=400\,\mathrm{meV} and 𝑵𝟎​�=−𝟔𝟎𝟎​𝐦𝐞𝐕N_{0}\beta=-600\,\mathrm{meV} [24, 3].

The paramagnetic response of the Mn magnetic moments to the external field is modelled by the empirical law [24, 25, 3]

⟨𝐦⟩=−𝑺𝟎​𝐁|𝐁|​𝑩𝟓/𝟐​(𝟓𝟐​𝒈𝐌𝐧​�𝑩​|𝐁|𝒌𝑩​(𝑻+𝑻𝟎)),\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle=-S_{0}\frac{\mathbf{B}}{\lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert}B_{5/2}\left(\frac{\tfrac{5}{2}g_{\mathrm{Mn}}\mu_{B}\lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert}{k_{B}(T+T_{0})}\right), (58)

where 𝑩𝟓/𝟐B_{5/2} is the Brillouin function for spin 𝑱=𝟓𝟐J=\tfrac{5}{2},

𝑩𝑱​(𝒙)=𝟐​𝑱+𝟏𝟐​𝑱​𝐜𝐨𝐭𝐡⁡(𝟐​𝑱+𝟏𝟐​𝑱​𝒙)−𝟏𝟐​𝑱​𝐜𝐨𝐭𝐡⁡(𝟏𝟐​𝑱​𝒙).B_{J}(x)=\frac{2J+1}{2J}\coth\left(\frac{2J+1}{2J}x\right)-\frac{1}{2J}\coth\left(\frac{1}{2J}x\right). (59)

The effective total spin 𝑺𝟎=−𝟓𝟐S_{0}=-\frac{5}{2} and the temperature offset 𝑻𝟎T_{0} are material parameters. For historical reasons, we have used the value 𝑻𝟎=2.6​𝐊T_{0}=2.6\,\mathrm{K}, but recent experiments have proved that 𝑻𝟎T_{0} depends on the Mn content 𝒚y and is typically smaller than this value, especially for smaller 𝒚y [26]. In kdotpy, the values 𝒈𝐌𝐧g_{\mathrm{Mn}} and 𝑻𝟎T_{0} are treated as material parameter and need not be constant in the Mn content, though the default material definitions for Hg1-yMnyTe contain the 𝒚y-independent values for historical reasons.

2.6 Bulk inversion asymmetry

The terms in Hamiltonian 𝑯𝐊𝐚𝐧𝐞H_{\mathrm{Kane}} [Eq. (14)] are symmetric under spatial inversion, i.e., the transformation given by (𝒙,𝒚,𝒛)→(−𝒙,−𝒚,−𝒛)(x,y,z)\to(-x,-y,-z) and (𝒌𝒙,𝒌𝒚,𝒌𝒛)→(−𝒌𝒙,−𝒌𝒚,−𝒌𝒛)(k_{x},k_{y},k_{z})\to(-k_{x},-k_{y},-k_{z}). For 𝑯𝐊𝐚𝐧𝐞H_{\mathrm{Kane}}, the relevant point group is 𝑶𝒉O_{h}. However, the zincblende crystal structure is not symmetric under inversion; it has point group 𝑻𝒅T_{d}. This means that terms breaking spatial inversion symmetry are allowed to appear in the Hamiltonian. Indeed, bulk-inversion asymmetry (BIA) is known to affect the band structure, although the inversion symmetric terms remain dominant. In other words, bulk-inversion asymmetry can be treated as a perturbation to the inversion symmetric Hamiltonian 𝑯𝐊𝐚𝐧𝐞H_{\mathrm{Kane}}.

From representation theory of the point group 𝑻𝒅T_{d}, it can be derived which BIA terms are permitted. Like before, we consider only those terms up to quadratic order in momentum. There is a single independent term linear in momentum, given by the Hamiltonian blocks [15]

𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟖𝟖=𝑪​(𝟎−𝟏𝟐​𝒌+𝒌𝒛−𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝒌−−𝟏𝟐​𝒌−𝟎𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝒌+−𝒌𝒛𝒌𝒛𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝒌−𝟎−𝟏𝟐​𝒌+−𝟏𝟐​𝟑​𝒌+−𝒌𝒛−𝟏𝟐​𝒌−𝟎),𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟖𝟕=𝟏𝟐​𝟐​𝑪​(𝒌+𝟐​𝒌𝒛𝟎−𝟑​𝒌+𝟑​𝒌−𝟎𝟐​𝒌𝒛−𝒌−),H_{\mathrm{BIA},88}=C\begin{pmatrix}0&-\frac{1}{2}k_{+}&k_{z}&-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}k_{-}\\ -\frac{1}{2}k_{-}&0&\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}k_{+}&-k_{z}\\ k_{z}&\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}k_{-}&0&-\frac{1}{2}k_{+}\\ -\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}k_{+}&-k_{z}&-\frac{1}{2}k_{-}&0\end{pmatrix},\hskip 22.99988ptH_{\mathrm{BIA},87}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}C\begin{pmatrix}k_{+}&2k_{z}\\ 0&-\sqrt{3}k_{+}\\ \sqrt{3}k_{-}&0\\ 2k_{z}&-k_{-}\end{pmatrix}, (60)

and 𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟕𝟖=𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟖𝟕†H_{\mathrm{BIA,78}}=H_{\mathrm{BIA,87}}^{\dagger}. The coefficient 𝑪C is the material parameter for the strength of linear BIA. There are three independent quadratic terms, given by

𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟔𝟖\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{BIA},68} =𝟏𝟔​𝑩𝟖+​(𝟑​𝒌−​𝒌𝒛𝟐​𝐢​𝒌𝒙​𝒌𝒚𝒌+​𝒌𝒛𝟎𝟎𝒌−​𝒌𝒛𝟐​𝐢​𝒌𝒙​𝒌𝒚𝟑​𝒌+​𝒌𝒛)+𝟏𝟑​𝟐​𝑩𝟖−​(𝟎𝟑​𝑲𝟒𝟎𝑲𝟓−𝑲𝟓𝟎−𝟑​𝑲𝟒𝟎)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}B_{8+}\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{3}k_{-}k_{z}&2\mathrm{i}k_{x}k_{y}&k_{+}k_{z}&0\\ 0&k_{-}k_{z}&2\mathrm{i}k_{x}k_{y}&\sqrt{3}k_{+}k_{z}\end{pmatrix}+\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}B_{8-}\begin{pmatrix}0&\sqrt{3}K_{4}&0&K_{5}\\ -K_{5}&0&-\sqrt{3}K_{4}&0\end{pmatrix}
𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟔𝟕\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{BIA},67} =𝟏𝟑​𝑩𝟕​(−𝐢​𝒌𝒙​𝒌𝒚−𝒌+​𝒌𝒛𝒌−​𝒌𝒛𝐢​𝒌𝒙​𝒌𝒚),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}B_{7}\begin{pmatrix}-\mathrm{i}k_{x}k_{y}&-k_{+}k_{z}\\ k_{-}k_{z}&\mathrm{i}k_{x}k_{y}\end{pmatrix}, (61)

where 𝑲𝟒≡𝒌𝒙𝟐−𝒌𝒚𝟐K_{4}\equiv k_{x}^{2}-k_{y}^{2} and 𝑲𝟓≡𝒌𝒙𝟐+𝒌𝒚𝟐−𝟐​𝒌𝒛𝟐K_{5}\equiv k_{x}^{2}+k_{y}^{2}-2k_{z}^{2}, and the coefficients 𝑩𝟖+B_{8+}, 𝑩𝟖−B_{8-}, and 𝑩𝟕B_{7} are material parameters. The blocks 𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟕𝟔H_{\mathrm{BIA},76} and 𝑯𝐁𝐈𝐀,𝟖𝟔H_{\mathrm{BIA},86} are given by the respective hermitian conjugates. The blocks 𝑯𝟔𝟔H_{66} and 𝑯𝟕𝟕H_{77} do not contain BIA terms up to quadratic order.

Representative values of the material parameters for CdTe [15, 27] and HgTe [28] are listed in Table 3. These values are also included as material parameters in kdotpy.

For nonzero magnetic fields, the BIA terms also lead to extra contributions from the Peierls substitution. For a strip geometry, this leads to extra contributions involving the gauge field 𝐀\mathbf{A} (see Sec. 2.3.1). In the Landau level formalism (see Sec. 2.4), additional ladder operators appear. For growth direction (001), this leads to terms coupling Landau levels with indices 𝒏,𝒏′n,n^{\prime} with 𝒏′−𝒏=±𝟐n^{\prime}-n=\pm 2. Whereas for the inversion symmetric LL Hamiltonian 𝒏𝐦𝐨𝐝𝟒n\mod 4 is a conserved quantum number, the BIA lowers this symmetry such that only 𝒏𝐦𝐨𝐝𝟐n\mod 2 remains conserved.

2.7 Strain

2.7.1 Strain and stress

The materials used in a heterostructure typically have slight differences in their equilibrium lattice constant. Two adjacent epitaxially grown layers can be strained as to match their in-plane lattice constants, if the mismatch between the equilibrium lattice constants is sufficiently small. This is known as pseudomorphic growth (see Ref. [29] and references therein). In practice, the in-plane lattice constant is generally determined by that of the substrate, which is usually much thicker than the epitaxial layers on top. If the epitaxial layers are too thick (more than a few hundred nm for HgTe and CdTe), relaxation occurs towards the equilibrium lattice constant.

The physical quantity strain is the deviation of the lattice constant of the strained layer 𝒂𝐬a_{\mathrm{s}} relative to the equilibrium lattice constant 𝒂𝟎a_{0}; in one dimension, strain is the dimensionless quantity

�=𝒂𝒔−𝒂𝟎𝒂𝟎.\epsilon=\frac{a_{s}-a_{0}}{a_{0}}. (62)

In a three-dimensional crystal, strain leads to a displacement of each of the three lattice vectors 𝐚𝒊\mathbf{a}_{i} (𝒊=𝒙,𝒚,𝒛i=x,y,z in a crystal with cubic symmetry). The displacement can be written in terms of a tensor 𝑨𝒊​𝒋A_{ij}, which satisfies [30]

𝐚𝒊,𝒔=∑𝒋=𝟏𝟑(�𝒊​𝒋+𝑨𝒊​𝒋)​𝐚𝒋,𝟎,\mathbf{a}_{i,s}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}(\delta_{ij}+A_{ij})\mathbf{a}_{j,0}, (63)

where �𝒊​𝒋\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta. The non-rotational (i.e., symmetrical) part of 𝑨𝒊​𝒋A_{ij} is the strain tensor

�𝒊​𝒋=𝟏𝟐​(𝑨𝒊​𝒋+𝑨𝒋​𝒊).\epsilon_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(A_{ij}+A_{ji}). (64)

The strain tensor �𝒊​𝒋\epsilon_{ij} is symmetric by definition. The diagonal terms �𝒊​𝒊\epsilon_{ii} represent linear strain and the off-diagonal terms �𝒙​𝒚,�𝒚​𝒛,�𝒛​𝒙\epsilon_{xy},\epsilon_{yz},\epsilon_{zx} represent shear strain.

A strained crystal is not in equilibrium and thus experiences forces that pushes the crystal back to its equilibrium lattice constant, or conversely, external forces are needed to bring a crystal into a strained state. Here, we consider the linear response regime, where Hooke’s law is valid, i.e., the force 𝑭F and the displacement 𝒖u are linearly proportional, 𝑭=𝒌​𝒖F=ku, with the stiffness constant 𝒌k. The generalization of Hooke’s law to a crystal in three dimensions relates the stress tensor �𝒊​𝒋\sigma_{ij} to the strain tensor �𝒌​𝒍\epsilon_{kl} as

�𝒊​𝒋=∑𝒌,𝒍=𝟏𝟑𝑺𝒊​𝒋​𝒌​𝒍​�​𝒌​𝒍,\sigma_{ij}=\sum_{k,l=1}^{3}S_{ijkl}\epsilon{kl}, (65)

in terms of the stiffness tensor 𝑪𝒊​𝒋​𝒌​𝒍C_{ijkl}. The stiffness tensor is a rank-4 tensor with 𝟖𝟏=𝟑×𝟑×𝟑×𝟑81=3\times 3\times 3\times 3 components (also known as elasticity modules). The stress tensor and stiffness tensor (elasticity modules) both carry the units of pressure, typically 𝐆𝐏𝐚\mathrm{GPa} in this context.

For a crystal with cubic symmetry, the stiffness tensor has only 𝟑3 independent components [30]. If the strain and stress tensors are vectorized as �~=(�𝒙​𝒙,�𝒚​𝒚,�𝒛​𝒛,𝟐​�𝒚​𝒛,𝟐​�𝒛​𝒙,𝟐​�𝒙​𝒚)\tilde{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_{xx},\epsilon_{yy},\epsilon_{zz},2\epsilon_{yz},2\epsilon_{zx},2\epsilon_{xy}) and �~=(�𝒙​𝒙,�𝒚​𝒚,�𝒛​𝒛,�𝒚​𝒛,�𝒛​𝒙,�𝒙​𝒚)\tilde{\sigma}=(\sigma_{xx},\sigma_{yy},\sigma_{zz},\sigma_{yz},\sigma_{zx},\sigma_{xy}), respectively, Eq. (65) can be written as �~=𝑪~​�~\tilde{\sigma}=\tilde{C}\tilde{\epsilon} in terms of the elasticity matrix

𝑪~=(𝑪𝟏𝟏𝑪𝟏𝟐𝑪𝟏𝟐𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑪𝟏𝟐𝑪𝟏𝟏𝑪𝟏𝟐𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑪𝟏𝟐𝑪𝟏𝟐𝑪𝟏𝟏𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑪𝟒𝟒𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑪𝟒𝟒𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑪𝟒𝟒).\tilde{C}=\begin{pmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}&C_{12}&0&0&0\\ C_{12}&C_{11}&C_{12}&0&0&0\\ C_{12}&C_{12}&C_{11}&0&0&0\\ 0&0&0&C_{44}&0&0\\ 0&0&0&0&C_{44}&0\\ 0&0&0&0&0&C_{44}\end{pmatrix}. (66)

The three independent components 𝑪𝟏𝟏C_{11}, 𝑪𝟏𝟐C_{12}, and 𝑪𝟒𝟒C_{44} are material parameters that can be found in the literature.

2.7.2 Strain Hamiltonian

The effect of strain on the band structure is formalized in the Bir-Pikus formalism [31]: The strain Hamiltonian is obtained from the 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} Hamiltonian by substitution of all terms quadratic in momentum as

𝒌𝒊​𝒌𝒋→�𝒊​𝒋k_{i}k_{j}\to\epsilon_{ij} (67)

and changing the band mass parameters 𝑭F, 1,2,3 to the deformation potentials (i.e., strain coefficients) 𝑪𝟏C_{1}, 𝑫𝒅D_{d}, 𝑫𝒖D_{u}, and 𝑫𝒖′D_{u}^{\prime} [2, 3, 15]. Taking Eq. (15) as a starting point, we find the strain Hamiltonian

𝑯𝐬=(𝑻𝐬𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑻𝐬𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑼𝐬+𝑽𝐬𝑺𝐬𝑹𝐬𝟎−𝟏𝟐​𝑺𝐬−𝟐​𝑹𝐬𝟎𝟎𝑺𝐬∗𝑼𝐬−𝑽𝐬𝟎𝑹𝐬𝟐​𝑽𝐬𝟑𝟐​𝑺𝐬𝟎𝟎𝑹𝐬∗𝟎𝑼𝐬−𝑽𝐬−𝑺𝐬𝟑𝟐​𝑺𝐬∗−𝟐​𝑽𝐬𝟎𝟎𝟎𝑹𝐬∗−𝑺𝐬∗𝑼𝐬+𝑽𝐬𝟐​𝑹𝐬∗−𝟏𝟐​𝑺𝐬∗𝟎𝟎−𝟏𝟐​𝑺𝐬∗𝟐​𝑽𝐬𝟑𝟐​𝑺𝐬𝟐​𝑹𝐬𝑼𝐬𝟎𝟎𝟎−𝟐​𝑹𝐬∗𝟑𝟐​𝑺𝐬∗−𝟐​𝑽𝐬−𝟏𝟐​𝑺𝐬𝟎𝑼𝐬)H_{\mathrm{s}}=\begin{pmatrix}T_{\mathrm{s}}&0&0&0&0&0&0&0\\ 0&T_{\mathrm{s}}&0&0&0&0&0&0\\ 0&0&U_{\mathrm{s}}+V_{\mathrm{s}}&S_{\mathrm{s}}&R_{\mathrm{s}}&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}S_{\mathrm{s}}&-\sqrt{2}R_{\mathrm{s}}\\ 0&0&S^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&U_{\mathrm{s}}-V_{\mathrm{s}}&0&R_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{2}V_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}S_{\mathrm{s}}\\ 0&0&R^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&0&U_{\mathrm{s}}-V_{\mathrm{s}}&-S_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}S^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&-\sqrt{2}V_{\mathrm{s}}\\ 0&0&0&R_{\mathrm{s}}^{*}&-S^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&U_{\mathrm{s}}+V_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{2}R^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}S^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}\\ 0&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}S^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{2}V_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}S_{\mathrm{s}}&\sqrt{2}R_{\mathrm{s}}&U_{\mathrm{s}}&0\\ 0&0&-\sqrt{2}R_{\mathrm{s}}^{*}&\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}S^{*}_{\mathrm{s}}&-\sqrt{2}V_{\mathrm{s}}&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}S_{\mathrm{s}}&0&U_{\mathrm{s}}\end{pmatrix} (68)

with

𝑻𝐬\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{s}} =𝑪𝟏​tr⁡�\displaystyle=C_{1}\tr\epsilon
𝑼𝐬\displaystyle U_{\mathrm{s}} =𝑫𝒅​tr⁡�,\displaystyle=D_{d}\tr\epsilon, 𝑹𝐬\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{s}} =𝟏𝟑​𝑫𝒖​(�𝒙​𝒙−�𝒚​𝒚)−𝟐𝟑​𝑫𝒖′​𝐢​�𝒙​𝒚,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}D_{u}(\epsilon_{xx}-\epsilon_{yy})-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}D_{u}^{\prime}\mathrm{i}\epsilon_{xy}, (69)
𝑽𝐬\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{s}} =−𝟏𝟑​𝑫𝒖​(�𝒙​𝒙+�𝒚​𝒚−𝟐​�𝒛​𝒛),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{3}D_{u}(\epsilon_{xx}+\epsilon_{yy}-2\epsilon_{zz}), 𝑺𝐬\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{s}} =𝟐𝟑​𝑫𝒖′​(�𝒙​𝒛−𝐢​�𝒚​𝒛),\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}D_{u}^{\prime}(\epsilon_{xz}-\mathrm{i}\epsilon_{yz}),

where tr⁡�=�𝒙​𝒙+�𝒚​𝒚+�𝒛​𝒛\tr\epsilon=\epsilon_{xx}+\epsilon_{yy}+\epsilon_{zz}. The values of the deformation potentials 𝑪𝟏C_{1}, 𝑫𝒅D_{d}, 𝑫𝒖D_{u}, and 𝑫𝒖′D_{u}^{\prime} for HgTe and CdTe that have been provided with kdotpy, are listed in Table 4 and have been taken from Ref. [2]. We note that this and other literature sources (e.g., Ref. [31]) use the alternative set of deformation potentials 𝑪=𝑪𝟏C=C_{1}, 𝒂=𝑫𝒅a=D_{d}, 𝒃=−𝟐𝟑​𝑫𝒖b=-\frac{2}{3}D_{u} and 𝒅=−𝟐𝟑​𝑫𝒖′d=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}D_{u}^{\prime}.

Symmetry allows further terms in the strain Hamiltonian. For example, application of the Bir-Pikus substitution to cubic momentum terms leads to strain terms linear in strain and momentum, i.e., involving linear combinations of �𝒊​𝒋​𝒌𝒍\epsilon_{ij}k_{l}. (See the tables in Ref. [15] for examples of these terms.) Here, we neglect these ‘higher-order’ terms, as they are negligible for these materials [2]. For a systematic study of these higher-order strain terms, we refer to Ref. [32].

2.8 Topology

2.8.1 Berry connection, Berry curvature, Chern number

The topological character of a material is typically understood theoretically in terms of the Chern number of the bands. In a nutshell, band inversion can cause the Chern numbers to become non-trivial, which leads to measurable signatures in the Hall conductance.

A common picture to understand the concept of a Chern number is the analogy with a winding number of the spin of a spin-𝟏𝟐\frac{1}{2} particle [33]. The spin eigenstate | (𝐤)⟩\lvert\psi(\mathbf{k})\rangle can be represented by a momentum dependent vector 𝐝⁡(𝐤)\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k}) on the Bloch sphere. Then one can consider the area swept out by 𝐝⁡(𝐤)\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k}) where the momenta 𝐤\mathbf{k} span the complete Brillouin zone. The signed area is 𝟒​�​𝑪4\pi C, i.e., the area 𝟒​�4\pi of the unit sphere times the Chern number 𝑪C. If the Brillouin zone is finite, the Chern number is integer, whereas for the continuum limit of infinitely large Brillouin zones, it may also be half-integer.

The above picture can be formalized in terms of concepts from differential geometry. If we consider an eigenstate | (𝐤)⟩\lvert\psi(\mathbf{k})\rangle that is differentiable in the Brillouin zone, we can define the Berry connection [33]

𝐀( )​(𝐤)=𝐢⁡⟨ ​(𝐤)|∇𝐤| ​(𝐤)⟩\mathbf{A}^{(\psi)}(\mathbf{k})=\mathrm{i}\langle\psi(\mathbf{k})|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}|\psi(\mathbf{k})\rangle (70)

at each point 𝐤\mathbf{k}. This quantity is analogous to the magnetic vector potential, hence it also goes by the name Berry vector potential [33]. The Berry phase is an integral of the Berry curvature over the closed contour 𝓒\mathcal{C} that surrounds the Brillouin zone,

=( )∫𝓒𝒅𝐤⋅𝐀( )(𝐤).{}^{(\psi)}=\int_{\mathcal{C}}d\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{A}^{(\psi)}(\mathbf{k}). (71)

The Berry phase is an integer number times 𝟐​�2\pi, which defines the Chern number 𝑪( )C^{(\psi)} as ( )=𝟐�𝑪( ){}^{(\psi)}=2\pi C^{(\psi)} [33].

The integral of Eq. (71) can be rewritten by virtue of Stokes’ theorem as an integral over the interior 𝓢\mathcal{S} of the Brillouin zone,

=( )∫𝓢𝒅𝐒⋅∇𝐤×𝐀( )(𝐤)≡∫𝓢𝒅𝐒⋅(𝐤)( ),{}^{(\psi)}=\int_{\mathcal{S}}d\mathbf{S}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\times\mathbf{A}^{(\psi)}(\mathbf{k})\equiv\int_{\mathcal{S}}d\mathbf{S}\cdot{}^{(\psi)}(\mathbf{k}), (72)

where 𝒅​𝐒d\mathbf{S} is a surface element and (𝐤)( ){}^{(\psi)}(\mathbf{k}) is the Berry curvature, defined by (𝐤)( )=∇𝐤×𝐀( ){}^{(\psi)}(\mathbf{k})=\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\times\mathbf{A}^{(\psi)}, or in component notation (𝒊,𝒍,𝒎=𝟏,𝟐,𝟑i,l,m=1,2,3),

(𝐤)𝒊( )=∑𝒍,𝒎�𝒊​𝒍​𝒎𝑭𝒍​𝒎( )(𝐤){}^{(\psi)}_{i}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{l,m}\epsilon_{ilm}F^{(\psi)}_{lm}(\mathbf{k})\\ (73)

with

𝑭𝒍​𝒎( )​(𝐤)=∂𝒌𝒍𝐀𝒎( )​(𝐤)−∂𝒌𝒎𝐀𝒍( )​(𝐤)=𝐢⁡⟨∂𝒌𝒍 ​(𝐤)|∂𝒌𝒎 ​(𝐤)⟩−𝐢⁡⟨∂𝒌𝒎 ​(𝐤)|∂𝒌𝒍 ​(𝐤)⟩.F^{(\psi)}_{lm}(\mathbf{k})=\partial_{k_{l}}\mathbf{A}^{(\psi)}_{m}(\mathbf{k})-\partial_{k_{m}}\mathbf{A}^{(\psi)}_{l}(\mathbf{k})=\mathrm{i}\langle\partial_{k_{l}}\psi(\mathbf{k})|\partial_{k_{m}}\psi(\mathbf{k})\rangle-\mathrm{i}\langle\partial_{k_{m}}\psi(\mathbf{k})|\partial_{k_{l}}\psi(\mathbf{k})\rangle. (74)

The analogue of the Berry curvature in electrodynamics is the magnetic field 𝐁=∇×𝐀\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}.

In practice, the Berry connection is challenging to calculate numerically: The derivative is discretized, where we evaluate the eigenstates at 𝐤\mathbf{k} and 𝐤+𝒅​𝐤\mathbf{k}+d\mathbf{k}. However, the result of the numerical evaluation has an indefinite overall phase factor (𝑼⁡(𝟏)U(1) gauge factor) which can vary randomly even between two points 𝐤\mathbf{k} and 𝐤+𝒅​𝐤\mathbf{k}+d\mathbf{k} close in momentum space. In Ref. [33], the Berry curvature (𝐤)𝒊( ){}^{(\psi)}_{i}(\mathbf{k}) [Eqs. (73) and (74)] is rewritten by ‘insertion of one’, ∑′|⟩′⟨|′\sum_{{}^{\prime}}\lvert{}^{\prime}\rangle\langle{}^{\prime}\rvert. This manipulation eventually yields a gauge invariant form of the Berry curvature

(𝐤)𝒊( )=−𝐈𝐦∑′≠ ∑𝒍,𝒎�𝒊​𝒍​𝒎⟨′(𝐤)|(∂𝒌𝒍𝑯)| (𝐤)⟩⟨ (𝐤)|(∂𝒌𝒎𝑯)|′(𝐤)⟩(𝑬′−𝑬)𝟐,{}^{(\psi)}_{i}(\mathbf{k})=-\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\sum_{{}^{\prime}\not=\psi}\sum_{l,m}\frac{\epsilon_{ilm}\langle{}^{\prime}(\mathbf{k})|(\partial_{k_{l}}H)|\psi(\mathbf{k})\rangle\langle\psi(\mathbf{k})|(\partial_{k_{m}}H)|{}^{\prime}(\mathbf{k})\rangle}{(E_{{}^{\prime}}-E)^{2}}, (75)

where the summation is over all states in the spectrum other than | ⟩\lvert\psi\rangle itself, and 𝑬E and 𝑬′E_{{}^{\prime}} are the energy eigenvalues. This expression is manifestly 𝑼⁡(𝟏)U(1) invariant, as all phase factors from the eigenstates come in conjugate pairs. The momentum derivatives of the Hamiltonian ∂𝒌𝒍𝑯\partial_{k_{l}}H (𝒍=𝟏,𝟐,𝟑l=1,2,3) can be evaluated analytically or numerically; even for the numerical derivative, there are no indefinite phase factors to be taken care of.

2.8.2 Hall conductance

The bulk-boundary theorem (see, e.g., Ref. [33]) connects the Chern numbers to the Hall conductance �𝐇=�𝒙​𝒚\sigma_{\mathrm{H}}=\sigma_{xy} of a device in a magnetic field, as

�𝐇=𝒆𝟐𝒉​∑occupied states ​ 𝑪( ).\sigma_{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{e^{2}}{h}\sum_{\text{occupied states }\psi}C^{(\psi)}. (76)

That is, the sum of the Chern numbers of the occupied bands yields the Hall conductance in units of the conductance quantum 𝒆𝟐/𝒉e^{2}/h. This result can be used to find the Hall conductance �𝐇\sigma_{\mathrm{H}} in a Landau fan: For each additional occupied Landau level, the Hall conductance is increased by 𝑪( )​𝒆𝟐/𝒉C^{(\psi)}e^{2}/h. Typically, 𝑪( )=𝟏C^{(\psi)}=1 for all Landau levels, so that finding the Hall conductance simplifies to a mere counting problem of occupied states. In kdotpy, the Hall conductance can be determined either with Chern numbers calculated with Eq. (75) or with simulated Chern numbers based on the assumption that 𝑪( )=𝟏C^{(\psi)}=1. The implementation is discussed in more detail in Sec. 3.5.3.

3 Implementation

3.1 Overview of the program

3.1.1 General remarks

Like its name suggests, kdotpy implements 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} theory in a Python program. The program is designed as a command-line interface (CLI): The operation of the program is determined primarily by a sequence of command line arguments entered by the user on the shell (e.g., bash). Moreover, the behaviour and output can be adjusted with configuration settings.

3.1.2 Package structure

The kdotpy application is actually a collection of several subprograms, that do the actual work. Most of these subprograms are Python scripts themselves. The subprograms are referred to by the first two arguments on the command line, for example kdotpy 2d. The command kdotpy invokes the main script main.py (provided that the kdotpy module has been installed successfully with PIP, see Section 4). In this example, main.py imports kdotpy-2d.py and runs its main() function. The latter contains the ‘recipe’ of this subprogram, which we will discuss in greater detail in Sec. 3.1.3.

The kdotpy module defines five subprograms that we classify as calculation subprograms, because they do the actual computational work: constructing a Hamiltonian, diagonalizing it, and processing the eigenvalues and eigenstates.

  • •

    kdotpy 2d: Calculates a dispersion of a structure with two translational degrees of freedom. The 𝒛z direction is kept spatial and is appropriately discretized. A typical configuration for this case is a quantum well.

  • •

    kdotpy 1d: Calculates a dispersion of a structure with one translational degree of freedom, for example a Hall bar. The 𝒚y and 𝒛z direction are kept spatial and are discretized. Due to the very large size of the problem, it usually makes sense to run this subprogram on a cluster that supports ‘jobs’ with large memory requirements.

  • •

    kdotpy ll: Calculates a Landau level spectrum for a configuration similar to the ‘2D’ mode, using the Landau level formalism of Sec. 2.4.

  • •

    kdotpy bulk: Calculates the dispersion for the ‘bulk’, i.e., with translational degrees of freedom in all 𝟑3 directions.

  • •

    kdotpy bulk-ll: Calculates a Landau level spectrum for a geometry with translational symmetry in the 𝒛z direction.

The package also contains several auxiliary subprograms for several other tasks other than doing the actual calculations:

  • •

    kdotpy merge: This subprogram is used for re-plotting data from earlier runs of kdotpy. It takes as input one or more XML files. The name kdotpy merge derives from the fact that it can be used to merge several data files, and show all results in a single plot.

  • •

    kdotpy compare: Similar to kdotpy merge, but shows data files (or sets of data files) using different colours/symbols in a single plot.

  • •

    kdotpy batch: A simple tool for running batch calculations with kdotpy, for example iterating a calculation while varying one of the input parameters. This subprogram serves a similar purpose as a shell script, but has a convenient monitor that shows the estimated time at which the calculations will finish.

  • •

    kdotpy test: Test suite. This tool runs all standardized tests or a selection of them, as to test whether kdotpy runs properly.

  • •

    kdotpy config: For viewing and modifying the configuration settings.

  • •

    kdotpy help: Show the built-in help file (with command line and configuration option reference) in a terminal viewer. With kdotpy help item, can search for a specific item in the help file.

  • •

    kdotpy doc: With kdotpy doc object, one gets developer information on the given object, e.g., a function or class. This tool shows the relevant docstring on the terminal.

  • •

    kdotpy version: Show the version of kdotpy.

The final three are not separate Python scripts, but functions called directly from the main program. For detailed instructions on how to use kdotpy from the command line, we refer to Sec. 5.

The Python code is structured as follows. The root directory of contains the metadata, such as the pyproject.toml file, the README.md file and the license text. The code itself is found in the subdirectory src/kdotpy. This directory contains the main module (in main.py), the scripts for the subprograms, and several other source files that are imported by the subprograms. Inside src/kdotpy, the following subdirectories collect several larger components of the program:

  • •

    bandalign: For band alignment, see Sec. 3.6.

  • •

    cmdargs: Functions that parse the command line arguments, see Sec. 3.2.1.

  • •

    density: Functions for calculating carrier density, density of states, etc., see Sec. 3.7.

  • •

    diagonalization: The infrastructure for diagonalization of the Hamiltonians, see Sec. 3.4.

  • •

    hamiltonian: For construction of the Hamiltonians, see Sec. 3.3.

  • •

    materials: For parsing the files that contain the material parameters, see Sec. 3.2.4.

  • •

    ploto: For plot output, see Sec. 3.10.4.

  • •

    tableo: For table output, see Sec. 3.10.3.

  • •

    xmlio: For XML input and output, see Sec. 3.10.2.

The materials subdirectory also contains the default materials file. Finally, the built-in helpfile is located at docs/helpfile.txt inside src/kdotpy. The components will be discussed below in the remainder of Sec. 3, roughly in the order in which they are executed in a kdotpy calculation.

3.1.3 Calculation subprogram workflow

The five calculation subprograms differ substantially in the details, but they all follow a similar workflow, going through the same sequence of stages. Figure 1 illustrates a schematic flow diagram with the important stages. The sequence can be summarized as follows.

  • •

    Preprocessing:

    • –

      Parse command line arguments, read configuration values and material parameters

    • –

      Define electrostatic potential (read from file and/or calculated with the self-consistent Hartree method)

    • –

      Prepare for diagonalization (determine band characters, charge neutrality point (CNP))

  • •

    Diagonalization (iteration over 𝒌k or 𝑩B points):

    • –

      Construct Hamiltonian

    • –
